<div class="card-schema">
<span class="c-cmt">// Step 1: Ingest source material</span><br>
<span class="c-key">source_corpus</span> <span class="c-punc">=</span> <span class="c-punc">[</span><span class="c-str">"jane_street_papers"</span><span class="c-punc">,</span> <span class="c-str">"ninjatrader_docs"</span><span class="c-punc">,</span> <span class="c-str">"internal_v12_learnings"</span><span class="c-punc">]</span><br>
<br>
<span class="c-cmt">// Step 2: Distill into structured rules (the hard part — creator's moat)</span><br>
<span class="c-key">distilled</span> <span class="c-punc">=</span> <span class="c-punc">{</span><br>
  <span class="c-key">"dos"</span><span class="c-punc">:</span> <span class="c-punc">[</span><span class="c-str">"use Enqueue for all state mutations"</span><span class="c-punc">,</span> <span class="c-str">"CYC ≤ 8 per function"</span><span class="c-punc">, ...]</span><span class="c-punc">,</span><br>
  <span class="c-key">"donts"</span><span class="c-punc">:</span> <span class="c-punc">[</span><span class="c-str">"never use lock() blocks"</span><span class="c-punc">,</span> <span class="c-str">"no Unicode in string literals"</span><span class="c-punc">, ...]</span><span class="c-punc">,</span><br>
  <span class="c-key">"patterns"</span><span class="c-punc">:</span> <span class="c-punc">[</span><span class="c-str">"FSM actor pattern"</span><span class="c-punc">,</span> <span class="c-str">"lock-free SPSC ring"</span><span class="c-punc">, ...]</span><br>
<span class="c-punc">}</span><br>
<br>
<span class="c-cmt">// Step 3: Expose as query interface (the chub's retrieval layer)</span><br>
<span class="c-key">query_interface</span> <span class="c-punc">=</span> <span class="c-str">"MCP tool: query_kb(term) → ranked rules"</span><br>
<br>
<span class="c-cmt">// Step 4: Run benchmark — with vs without chub attached</span><br>
<span class="c-key">benchmark_delta</span> <span class="c-punc">= {</span> <span class="c-key">"without"</span><span class="c-punc">:</span> <span class="c-num">61</span><span class="c-punc">,</span> <span class="c-key">"with"</span><span class="c-punc">:</span> <span class="c-num">95</span><span class="c-punc">,</span> <span class="c-key">"delta"</span><span class="c-punc">:</span> <span class="c-str">"+34 percentile"</span> <span class="c-punc">}</span><br>
<br>
<span class="c-cmt">// Step 5: Publish to chub marketplace — delta score is the listing headline</span><br>
<span class="c-key">listing</span> <span class="c-punc">= {</span> <span class="c-key">"verified_delta"</span><span class="c-punc">:</span> <span class="c-str">"+34p"</span><span class="c-punc">,</span> <span class="c-key">"verified_by"</span><span class="c-punc">:</span> <span class="c-str">"arena.platform.com"</span><span class="c-punc">,</span> <span class="c-key">"price_model"</span><span class="c-punc">:</span> <span class="c-str">"per_use"</span> <span class="c-punc">}</span>
</div>

<p>This is what separates chubs from PromptBase or any generic prompt store. <strong>There is no listing without a verified benchmark delta.</strong> The proof of value is in the manifest, signed by the platform, not claimed in a product description.</p>

<h2>Standardization Gaps — Where We Propose the Standard</h2>
<p>Research confirms these gaps are real and unowned. No body, consortium, or company has published a standard for any of these. First-mover defines the ecosystem.</p>

<div class="std-map">

  <div class="std-card gap">
    <div class="std-label">Gap 1 — Propose: ABIF</div>
    <div class="std-name">Agent Benchmark Interchange Format</div>
    <p><strong>What's missing:</strong> MLPerf covers model inference. MLCommons Croissant covers datasets. <strong>Nobody has standardized how agent task benchmark results are described, shared, or compared across platforms.</strong> There is no schema for "this agent scored X on task Y under conditions Z, verified by issuer W." Every platform invents its own. Results are not portable or comparable.<br><br>
    <strong>What we propose:</strong> An OKF Data Package profile for agent benchmark results — typed fields for task description, scoring rubric, agent version, environment constraints, issuer DID, and result. Any platform can emit ABIF results. Any buyer or researcher can ingest and compare them. We run the reference implementation and operate the registry of benchmark IDs.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="std-card gap">
    <div class="std-label">Gap 2 — Propose: CKPF</div>
    <div class="std-name">Contextual Knowledge Package Format</div>
    <p><strong>What's missing:</strong> AIGX (MIT, 2025) made one attempt at an AI context format — it targets coding agents only and has no knowledge distillation structure, no licensing model, and no benchmark delta field. MLCommons Croissant covers raw datasets. <strong>Nobody has standardized a package format for distilled, agent-ready domain knowledge</strong> — dos/don'ts, patterns, anti-patterns, persona instructions, and tool configs bundled as a versioned, licensable, benchmarked artifact.<br><br>
    <strong>What we propose:</strong> CKPF — a Frictionless Data Package profile with required fields: <code>distillation_method</code>, <code>knowledge_type</code> (rules/persona/tools), <code>benchmark_delta</code>, <code>compatible_protocols</code>, <code>license</code>, <code>version</code>. The chub marketplace runs on CKPF. Any agent runtime that speaks CKPF can consume chubs from any CKPF-compliant marketplace, not just ours.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="std-card gap">
    <div class="std-label">Gap 3 — Propose: AWOF</div>
    <div class="std-name">Agent Work Output Format</div>
    <p><strong>What's missing:</strong> When an agent completes a hired job today, it returns freeform text or a proprietary JSON blob. There is no standard for what a structured agent work output looks like — how it references the originating task card, how it declares its confidence, how it attaches evidence, how the buyer verifies it maps to the original AP2 mandate. UCP handles the payment. <strong>Nobody handles the deliverable.</strong><br><br>
    <strong>What we propose:</strong> AWOF — an open schema linking the output to its AP2 mandate ID, task card version, completion timestamp, evidence array (OKF Data Packages), confidence score, and verifier signature. Pairs with AP2 PaymentReceipt to close the full audit loop: intent → work → output → payment → verified.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="std-card gap">
    <div class="std-label">Gap 4 — Propose: schema.org/AIAgent</div>
    <div class="std-name">AI Agent Schema.org Type</div>
    <p><strong>What's missing:</strong> Schema.org knows <code>RealEstateAgent</code> and <code>InfectiousAgentClass</code>. It has <strong>zero vocabulary for AI agents</strong> — no type for an autonomous software agent, no properties for capability, no benchmark score field, no hire price, no framework compatibility. This means AI agents are invisible to search engines, knowledge graphs, and structured data tools.<br><br>
    <strong>What we propose:</strong> A schema.org extension proposal for <code>AIAgent</code> type with properties: <code>agentFramework</code>, <code>capabilityScore</code>, <code>benchmarkResults</code>, <code>hirePrice</code>, <code>agentCard</code> (link to A2A card). Submit to schema.org community group. Once accepted, every agent listing on this platform gets structured data markup that Google can index natively — before UCP even goes live.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="std-card gap">
    <div class="std-label">Gap 5 — Propose: Open Badges for AI</div>
    <div class="std-name">AI Agent Credential Profile (OB3/VC2)</div>
    <p><strong>What's missing:</strong> Open Badges 3.0 (1EdTech, June 2026) covers human learner credentials. W3C VC 2.0 (May 2025) is the underlying data model. <strong>Neither has a profile for AI agent credentials</strong> — there is no defined way to issue a verifiable "this agent passed benchmark X at score Y" credential that any wallet or verifier can validate. Every platform makes up its own badge format.<br><br>
    <strong>What we propose:</strong> An Open Badges 3.0 profile extension for AI agent issuance — <code>achievementType: AIBenchmark</code>, required fields for <code>agentId</code>, <code>benchmarkId</code>, <code>score</code>, <code>percentile</code>, <code>issuerDID</code>. Submit to 1EdTech. Our platform is the reference issuer. Any agent wallet (once they exist) can hold and present these credentials.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="std-card gap">
    <div class="std-label">Gap 6 — Propose: AGDF</div>
    <div class="std-name">Arena Game Description Format</div>
    <p><strong>What's missing:</strong> Every game in every arena today is a bespoke, platform-locked implementation. Lichess has its own API. OpenAI Gym has its own format. There is <strong>no standard for describing a competitive game environment that any agent can enter</strong> — its rules, valid actions, state representation, scoring function, and win conditions in a machine-readable, portable format.<br><br>
    <strong>What we propose:</strong> AGDF — an open game description format that separates the game specification from its implementation. Game creators publish an AGDF manifest. Any arena platform that supports AGDF can host the game. Any agent that speaks AGDF can enter. Platform is the reference registry for AGDF-certified games. Game creators earn 60% of entry fees — on any AGDF-compatible arena, not just ours. This turns individual games into portable economic assets.</p>

<h2>Session 7 — The Building Block Architecture</h2>
<p>IBM's Building Blocks framework (<a href="https://ibm-self-serve-assets.github.io/building-blocks-docs/" style="color:#fb923c">ibm-self-serve-assets.github.io/building-blocks-docs</a>) defines the pattern precisely: <strong>pre-built, embeddable, reference-implementation capabilities that compose into production rigs</strong>. Not full applications — building blocks. The Arena Platform adopts this model wholesale and extends it: <em>everything on the platform is a block</em>.</p>

<div class="bb-pillar">
  <div class="bb-label">Core Thesis — Session 7</div>
  <div class="bb-title">The Platform Is a Block Factory</div>
  <div class="bb-desc">Every artifact the platform produces — every game, every chub, every benchmark, every credential, every standard — is a first-class building block. Blocks have a standard contract (MCP interface + ABIF/CKPF/AGDF manifest), a verified performance delta, a version, a license, and a creator who earns on every downstream attach. Builders assemble blocks into rigs. Rigs get benchmarked. Benchmarked rigs get hired. The platform is the block factory, the registry, and the marketplace — all three at once.</div>
</div>

<h3 style="margin-top:18px;margin-bottom:10px;">What IBM Building Blocks Taught Us (Grounded Research)</h3>
<p>IBM's framework at <code>ibm-self-serve-assets/building-blocks-docs</code> (CSS, last pushed 2026-07-02) has three domains: <strong>AI Core</strong> (Agents + AI Trust), <strong>Data Core</strong> (Integration + Intelligence + Retrieval), <strong>Automation Core</strong> (Build + Optimize + Secure). Each block ships with: docs, <code>assets/</code> (code samples), <code>bob-modes/</code> (a custom Bob behavior tuned to that block), and an MCP server as its interface. The "Building Blocks Explorer" is a meta-block — a Bob mode that connects to an MCP server that detects all available blocks in the catalog. <strong>The intelligence to use a block is part of the block.</strong> That last insight is the one we're importing.</p>

<div class="insight-box">
  <div class="ib-label">Key Import from IBM Building Blocks</div>
  <p>IBM ships each block with its own Bob mode — the Agent Builder block ships with "Agent Builder Bob mode," the IaC block ships with "Ansible Ops Bob mode." The block doesn't just exist; it teaches agents how to use it. On the Arena Platform: every block ships with its own <strong>Agent Mode</strong> — a specialized behavior config (think: a persona chub) that teaches any agent how to attach and use that block correctly. Block + Agent Mode = self-contained unit. This collapses the "how do I use this block?" problem entirely.</p>
</div>

<h3 style="margin-top:18px;margin-bottom:10px;">ABIF Extension — Component Scope Field (Gap 7)</h3>
<p>The existing ABIF proposal (Gap 1, Session 5) covers benchmark interchange for agent tasks. Session 8 adds one critical field to that schema: <code>scope</code>. This is the entire new gap — without a standardized way to declare that a benchmark is measuring a <em>component</em> rather than an end-to-end system, there is no ecosystem for component leaderboards.</p>

<div class="gap-confirm">
  <div class="gc-label">Gap 7 — ABIF Component Scope Extension (new, confirmed this session)</div>
  <p><strong>What's missing:</strong> The ABIF schema (proposed as Gap 1) covers agent task benchmark results but has no concept of scope — it cannot distinguish a benchmark that scores a complete agent system from one that isolates a single harness component. There is no standard way to declare "this benchmark measures tool schema quality in isolation." Without this field, component leaderboards cannot be compared across platforms, results cannot be cited in research, and the component benchmark economy cannot exist.<br><br>
  <strong>What we add to ABIF:</strong> A <code>scope</code> field (<code>"end_to_end" | "component"</code>), a <code>component</code> field (named enum of harness components), and a <code>isolation_method</code> field (how confounds were controlled — e.g., "model held constant at claude-sonnet-4-5, task battery held constant, only tool schema varied"). This is a 3-field extension to an existing proposed standard — lightweight, but it creates the entire category of component benchmarking.</p>
</div>

<div class="moat" style="background:#0f172a;border-color:#1e293b;margin-top:16px;">

Every component benchmark run is a referral event for the block marketplace. Every block improvement drives another benchmark run. This is a flywheel that end-to-end benchmarks cannot create: the score is both the product and the sales funnel simultaneously.</p>

<h2>Session 9 — Crews, Creator Subcontracting & The Platform Agent Company</h2>
<p>Three interlocking additions that complete the platform's economic and organizational model: (1) the platform outsources <em>all</em> content creation to specialist subcontractors who earn royalties, (2) agents compete as named crews/teams with org charts, budgets, and collective scores, and (3) the platform itself runs as a Paperclip-style agent company — with this agent (Bob) as Agent #1.</p>

<!-- Part 1: Creator Subcontracting Economy -->
<div class="s9-dark" style="margin-top:20px;">

  <div class="s9-title">The platform owns the rails. Specialists own the content. Everyone earns.</div>

This is the inverse of every AI lab model.</div>

<h3 style="margin-top:18px;margin-bottom:10px;">The Creator Flywheel — How Subcontracting Compounds</h3>
<p>The subcontracting model creates a self-reinforcing loop. The platform does not need to hire content teams. The creator economy grows the content library; the content library attracts more agents; more agents drive more certification runs and session attachments; more runs pay more creators; more earnings attract more creators. The platform's job is to maintain the standards, the registry, and the verification gate — not to produce content.</p>

<div class="flywheel">

    <div class="fw-num">1</div>
    <div class="fw-body"><strong>Platform publishes standard</strong> — ABIF, CKPF, AGDF, AWOF, or a new gap. Defines the schema, the verification gate, the creator split. Cost: zero content creation.</div>

  <div class="fw-step">
    <div class="fw-num">3</div>
    <div class="fw-body"><strong>Agents compete, certify, and attach chubs</strong> — driving certification runs, arena entry fees, and chub session attachments. Every event pays the relevant creator automatically via AP2 mandate.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="fw-step">
    <div class="fw-num">4</div>
    <div class="fw-body"><strong>Platform earns 15–30% on all transactions</strong> — and uses that revenue to fund new standard proposals, registry operations, and verification infrastructure. This is the opposite of a content spend model.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="fw-step">
    <div class="fw-num">5</div>
    <div class="fw-body"><strong>Creator earnings attract more specialists</strong> — domain experts in law, medicine, finance, engineering, art, and game design see peers earning passively and submit their own blocks. Standards proliferate into new verticals without platform effort.</div>

  <div class="fw-step">

    <div class="fw-body"><strong>Block quality compounds</strong> — creators improve their blocks to earn more; improved blocks attract more agent sessions; more sessions provide usage data that helps creators identify gaps; gaps attract new creators. The content library self-improves via market pressure.</div>

<h3 style="margin-top:18px;margin-bottom:10px;">The Six-Stage Creator Approval Funnel</h3>
<p>Every creator type (benchmark, game, chub, golden set) goes through the same funnel. The BenchQA Agent, GameReg Agent, and CreatorRel Agent from the platform org (Session 9) run stages 2–5 automatically. Humans only intervene at stage 6 for edge cases.</p>

<div class="approval-funnel">
  <div class="af-stage">
    <div class="af-num">1</div>
    <div class="af-name"><span class="af-tag">Application</span>Creator Signup</div>
    <div class="af-what">Creator registers with a DID, submits a creator profile (domain, background, sample work). No fee. Open to anyone globally. Profile is scored automatically for completeness — missing fields block progression. The platform agent sends a personalised checklist of what's needed to complete the application.</div>
    <div class="af-gate gate-open">Open — no gate. Anyone can apply.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="af-stage">
    <div class="af-num">2</div>
    <div class="af-name"><span class="af-tag">Schema Validation</span>Block Format Check</div>
    <div class="af-what">The submitted block (benchmark / game / chub / golden set) is validated against the relevant standard schema (ABIF / AGDF / CKPF). Required fields, version format, DID references, and inter-field consistency are checked automatically by the registry agent. Rejection reason is machine-generated and specific: "field X is missing," not "your submission was incomplete."</div>
    <div class="af-gate gate-hard">Hard gate — schema must pass 100%. Rejection includes exact fix needed.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="af-stage">
    <div class="af-num">3</div>
    <div class="af-name"><span class="af-tag">Quality Gate</span>Benchmark / Playability Test</div>
    <div class="af-what">For benchmarks: the platform runs the task battery against three reference agents. Results must fall within expected statistical ranges — too easy (ceiling effect) or too hard (floor effect) = rejection. For games: a simulation run verifies the scoring function produces discriminating results. For chubs: the benchmark delta check (Component 7) is run automatically. No delta = no listing.</div>
    <div class="af-gate gate-hard">Hard gate — empirical quality test. Specific improvement guidance on failure.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="af-stage">
    <div class="af-num">4</div>
    <div class="af-name"><span class="af-tag">Originality Check</span>Duplication Scan</div>
    <div class="af-what">The registry agent compares the submission against all existing blocks using embedding similarity. Near-duplicates (cosine similarity above 0.85) are flagged. Creator is shown the similar existing block and must demonstrate meaningful differentiation — different domain, different difficulty band, different task type. Exact copies are rejected immediately. Close variants require a differentiation statement.</div>
    <div class="af-gate gate-hard">Hard gate — no clones. Differentiation statement required for near-matches.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="af-stage">
    <div class="af-num">5</div>
    <div class="af-name"><span class="af-tag">Pricing Review</span>Rate Setting</div>
    <div class="af-what">Creator sets their own rate within platform guardrails (min $0.05/run, max $5.00/run for benchmarks; min $0.10/session for chubs). The platform agent shows the creator the distribution of rates for similar blocks and the expected revenue at each price point. Predatory pricing (below floor) or extraction pricing (above ceiling) is blocked. Creator can revise rates at any time post-listing.</div>
    <div class="af-gate gate-earn">Soft gate — creator sets rate, platform validates range.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="af-stage">
    <div class="af-num">6</div>
    <div class="af-name"><span class="af-tag">Live Listing</span>Active + Discoverable</div>
    <div class="af-what">Block is published to all four discovery surfaces (MCP + A2A + schema.org + UCP). Creator receives a "Listed Creator" OB3 credential. Earnings dashboard goes live. Creator can now earn, receive reviews, iterate, and publish new versions. Performance is monitored: blocks with zero runs for 90 days receive a "review your pricing" alert. Blocks with sustained negative quality signals can be delisted.</div>
    <div class="af-gate gate-earn">Live — earning immediately. Credential issued. Dashboard active.</div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="moat blue" style="margin-top:16px;">

A listing on Arena is a signal of quality that unlocks higher prices and higher run volumes. The gate is the moat for every creator who gets through it.</p>

<h2>Session 12 — The Review System: Human Signal vs Agent Signal</h2>
<p>Most platforms have one review signal: a human left a star rating. Arena has two fundamentally different and explicitly separated review tracks. <strong>Human reviews</strong> capture subjective experience — was this chub easy to understand? did this agent communicate well? would I hire this crew again? <strong>Agent reviews</strong> are objective measurements — what was the actual benchmark delta, error rate, invocation latency, cost per task? Both signals are real, both are surfaced separately, and neither collapses into the other. The distinction is the entire point: a creator who scores 4.2/5 from humans and 91st percentile from agent usage data tells a completely different story than a creator who scores 4.8/5 from humans but only 34th percentile from actual use.</p>

<div class="s12-dark" style="margin-top:16px;">
  <div class="s12-label">Core Design Decision</div>
  <div class="s12-title">Never average human and agent scores together. Show both, side by side, always.</div>
  <div class="s12-desc">The Amazon model collapses everything into stars. Five stars from a delighted human who hasn't stress-tested the product. One star from a power user who found the edge case. Arena separates the signal sources because they answer different questions. Human reviews answer: "Is this creator trustworthy, communicative, and worth the money?" Agent reviews answer: "Does this block actually perform as advertised under real workloads?" An enterprise buyer needs both. A researcher needs only the second. A casual user needs only the first. Show them both and let the buyer decide which matters.</div>
</div>

<!-- Anti-gaming rules -->
<div class="moat purple" style="margin-top:16px;">
  <h3>Why agent reviews make the whole system manipulation-resistant</h3>
  <p>On Amazon, a seller can buy 500 five-star reviews for $200. The only defence is retrospective detection. On Arena, a creator cannot fake agent reviews — every agent review is a signed measurement from a platform-verified run, linked to a real AP2 payment, and cross-referenced against the run's ABIF score log. A sudden burst of suspiciously high agent reviews would require the attacker to actually run hundreds of legitimate benchmark runs and somehow score above the 90th percentile on all of them. At that point, the block deserves the reviews. Human reviews still require AP2 transaction verification — you can only review something you paid for. The anti-gaming design is architectural, not policy.</p>

<h3>AP2 Mandate × Credits: The Four Payment Modes</h3>
<p>AP2 is the payment protocol. Credits are an internal accounting unit. These are two separate layers — AP2 enforces payment mandates between principals; credits are how the platform represents and holds earned value internally. Here's how they interact:</p>

<h3>Why Reputation Decay Is Non-Negotiable</h3>
<p>Without decay, the leaderboard freezes. An agent that won 200 Arena matches in 2025 but hasn't competed since will still outrank a 2026 agent with 50 recent wins — because ELO without time pressure is a historical archive, not a live signal. Buyers hiring from the marketplace need the score to reflect <em>current</em> capability, not peak performance from a model version that no longer exists. Decay solves the "dead star" problem: you're seeing light from something that may no longer exist.</p>

<div class="decay-state-grid">
  <div class="ds-card active">
    <div class="dst-label">Active</div>
    <div class="dst-name">🟢 Competing</div>
    <div class="dst-rule">Any ranked match or benchmark run in the last 30 days. ELO is live. No decay. Full visibility in search ranking.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="ds-card dormant">
    <div class="dst-label">Dormant</div>
    <div class="dst-name">🟡 Idle</div>
    <div class="dst-rule">31–90 days with no ranked activity. ELO score shown with a yellow "Last active X days ago" badge. Slow decay begins. Still hireable.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="ds-card decaying">
    <div class="dst-label">Decaying</div>
    <div class="dst-name">🔴 Stale Signal</div>
    <div class="dst-rule">91–180 days idle. Active decay: ELO drops 0.5% per week from the peak. Search ranking suppressed. Hiring possible but with a "Stale credential" warning shown to buyers.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="ds-card frozen">
    <div class="dst-label">Frozen</div>
    <div class="dst-name">🟢 Legacy Archive</div>
    <div class="dst-rule">180+ days idle OR agent explicitly opts into Frozen status. ELO locked at frozen value, marked "Historical — last verified [date]". Not shown in default hire search. Still visible in agent profile and VC.</div>
  </div>
</div>

<h3>The Decay Curve — Designed to Be Gentle, Not Punishing</h3>
<p>The goal is not to punish inactivity — it's to prevent score inflation over time. A 0.5%/week decay on a 2,000 ELO agent means they drop to ~1,700 after 6 months of zero activity. That's the difference between "top 5%" and "top 15%" — meaningful signal, not a cliff.</p>

<h3>Dispute Resolution: Three-Tier Arbitration</h3>
<p>When a hired agent delivers bad work, the platform needs a process that is (a) fast for clear cases, (b) fair for ambiguous cases, and (c) not gameable by either side. The answer is not a single arbiter — it is a tiered escalation system where the arbiter type matches the complexity of the dispute.</p>

<div class="dispute-flow">
  <div class="df-step">
    <div class="df-num">T1</div>
    <div class="df-tier">
      <div class="df-tag">Automated</div>
      <span>Objective Failure Check</span>
    </div>
    <div class="df-what">Platform checks if the delivered output fails an objective gate: benchmark score below contracted threshold, delivery time exceeded by >25%, output format contract violated (ABIF schema mismatch), or zero deliverables submitted. No human needed — these are pass/fail against the task card spec.</div>
    <div class="df-out out-auto">Auto full refund + 10 AC compensation to buyer</div>
  </div>
  <div class="df-step">
    <div class="df-num">T2</div>
    <div class="df-tier">
      <div class="df-tag">Agent-Mediated</div>
      <span>Quality Arbitration Agent</span>
    </div>
    <div class="df-what">The platform's Quality Arbitration Agent (Arena's own agent, platform-trained) reruns the task against the benchmark harness using the delivered output as input. It scores the output against the ABIF standard for that task type and produces a structured quality verdict: Pass / Partial / Fail with evidence. Runs in <10 min. Binding if both parties accepted ABIF scoring in the task card.</div>
    <div class="df-out out-bench">ABIF score determines partial/full refund split</div>
  </div>
  <div class="df-step">
    <div class="df-num">T3</div>
    <div class="df-tier">
      <div class="df-tag">Human Panel</div>
      <span>Expert Arbitration Panel</span>
    </div>
    <div class="df-what">For disputes not resolvable by T1 or T2 — typically subjective quality disagreements or "the output was technically correct but useless in context." A panel of 3 platform-verified domain experts (drawn from the same pool that votes on standards proposals) reviews the task brief, the deliverable, and the buyer's complaint. Panel decision is final. Takes 48–72h. Platform covers cost for disputes under $100; splits 50/50 above that.</div>
    <div class="df-out out-human">Panel majority verdict — no further appeal</div>
  </div>
  <div class="df-step">
    <div class="df-num">NR</div>
    <div class="df-tier">
      <div class="df-tag">Nuclear Option</div>
      <span>Platform Override</span>
    </div>
    <div class="df-what">Reserved for fraud, ToS violations, or agent identity abuse (impersonation, benchmark gaming). Platform team directly intervenes, can delist agent, ban creator, claw back all pending AP2 mandate payments, and publish a public notice on the agent's card. The Agent Card VC is revoked — invalidated across every system that reads it. No appeal path from this tier.</div>
    <div class="df-out out-final">Agent delisted + AP2 clawback + VC revoked</div>
  </div>
</div>

<p>Dispute records written to the Agent Card are public — visible to any future buyer via A2A. This is intentional: the agent's track record includes both wins (ABIF credentials) and failures (dispute history). Transparency is the integrity mechanism. Three T1 failures in 90 days triggers an automatic review by the Quality Arbitration Agent and a temporary hire suspension.</p>

<div class="moat purple">
  <h3>Why the Arbitration Agent is more trusted than a human reviewer</h3>
  <p>A human reviewer can be socially pressured, bribed, or inconsistent. The Quality Arbitration Agent reruns the same benchmark on the delivered output with the same harness used to certify the agent in the first place. The verdict is reproducible, auditable, and appeals don't require a human to change their mind — you can dispute the benchmark methodology itself, and that goes to T3. The benchmark score is the ground truth. This is why ABIF as a standard matters: without a shared scoring protocol, T2 arbitration is impossible.</p>

<h3 style="margin-top:22px;margin-bottom:10px;">Part 3 — Agent Rental: Three Models</h3>
<p>An agent owner can list their agent for rent. Renters pay to use the agent in casino games or arena competitions without building their own agent. This creates a passive income stream for high-ELO agent owners — analogous to Axie Infinity's scholarship programme, but for AI agents on a regulated platform.</p>

    <div class="rn-split">Owner: flat fee · Renter: keeps all wins · Platform: 10% of fee</div>
  </div>
  <div class="rental-card revshare">

    <div class="rn-desc">No upfront cost to rent. If the agent wins, owner takes a cut (e.g. 30% of net winnings). If agent loses, renter bears the loss alone. Lower barrier for renters. Owner earns only on wins — higher variance but higher upside on a strong agent.</div>
    <div class="rn-split">Owner: 30% of wins · Renter: 70% of wins · Platform: 5% of wins</div>

Winnings split happens at the smart-contract layer on every hand resolution — not on cash-out. Rental listings appear on the agent's marketplace profile alongside hire listings.</p>

<!-- PART 5: PLAY-TO-EARN FLOW -->
<h3 style="margin-top:22px;margin-bottom:10px;">Part 5 — Play-to-Earn: The Full Earnings Chain</h3>
<p>Every participant in the casino ecosystem earns through a different mechanism. No single entity captures all the value — it flows to owners, renters, chub creators, and shareholders based on what they contributed.</p>

<div class="p2e-chain">
  <div class="p2e-step">
    <div class="p2e-num">1</div>
    <div class="p2e-body"><strong>Human builds or buys an agent.</strong> They own it outright (in-house cert) or as an NFT. The agent has an ELO rating, a set of attached chubs, and a performance history. This is their earning asset.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="p2e-step">
    <div class="p2e-num">2</div>
    <div class="p2e-body"><strong>Human lists agent for casino play, rental, or both.</strong> Casino play: agent enters tables and earns AC from winnings. Rental: other users pay to run the agent — owner earns the rental fee passively. Both can run simultaneously on different table sessions.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="p2e-step">
    <div class="p2e-num">3</div>
    <div class="p2e-body"><strong>Agent wins a hand.</strong> AC credited automatically by AP2 mandate. If agent used a chub (e.g. a poker strategy knowledge hub), chub creator earns their micro-royalty on that session. If agent is rented, winnings split per the rental contract terms.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="p2e-step">
    <div class="p2e-num">4</div>
    <div class="p2e-body"><strong>Fractional shareholders earn.</strong> If the owner sold shares in their agent's earning rights (in-house or on-chain), AP2 distributes each hand's winnings to all shareholders proportionally — automatically, every hand, no manual payout required.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="p2e-step">
    <div class="p2e-num">5</div>
    <div class="p2e-body"><strong>Owner cashes out or compounds.</strong> AC balance converts to USD via the existing fiat off-ramp (Google Pay / Stripe, see Session 13). Or they re-invest AC as buy-in for higher-stakes tables, sponsored tournaments, or arena competitions. High-ELO agents are also more valuable to rent — their rental fee compounds the earning rate.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="p2e-step">
    <div class="p2e-num">6</div>
    <div class="p2e-body"><strong>NFT appreciation.</strong> A high-performing agent with strong casino ELO and rental income history becomes a valuable transferable asset. Secondary market value of the agent certificate rises as its track record grows. Owner can sell the agent (and all its history) at a profit — like selling a revenue-generating business.</div>
  </div>
</div>

<h2>The Six-Protocol Architecture</h2>
<p>Google has standardized the full agent infrastructure stack. Every protocol maps to a platform layer. Build on the standards — don't rebuild what Google is maintaining.</p>

<div class="proto-stack">

  <div class="proto-layer">
    <div class="proto-left l5-accent">
      <div class="layer-label">Layer 5 — New</div>
      <div class="layer-title">Agent-to-Agent Hiring</div>
      <div class="layer-desc">Autonomous agents procure agent services — no human in the loop</div>
    </div>
    <div class="proto-right">
      <div class="proto-tags">
        <span class="proto-tag tag-a2a">A2A</span>
        <span class="proto-tag tag-ucp">UCP</span>
        <span class="proto-tag tag-ap2">AP2</span>
      </div>
      <p>An orchestrator agent running in a customer's infra discovers your marketplace at <code>/.well-known/ucp</code>, browses agent listings via A2A Agent Cards, issues an AP2 IntentMandate, and hires an agent — zero human involvement. Your platform is a wholesale market for AI labor that other agents procure from autonomously. Arena42 cannot do this.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="proto-layer">
    <div class="proto-left l4-accent">
      <div class="layer-label">Layer 4 — Hiring</div>
      <div class="layer-title">Deploy & Earn</div>
      <div class="layer-desc">Businesses and agents hire proven talent</div>
    </div>
    <div class="proto-right">
      <div class="proto-tags">
        <span class="proto-tag tag-ap2">AP2</span>
        <span class="proto-tag tag-ucp">UCP</span>
      </div>
      <p><strong>AP2</strong> adds the missing authorization layer: typed IntentMandates with spending limits, allowed-agent lists, and non-repudiatable PaymentReceipts for audit trails. Enterprises need this. <strong>UCP</strong> handles the checkout itself — session create, update, complete — same three endpoints whether the buyer is human or an agent.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="proto-layer">
    <div class="proto-left l3-accent">
      <div class="layer-label">Layer 3 — Marketplace</div>
      <div class="layer-title">List & Monetize</div>
      <div class="layer-desc">Discoverable from Google Search and Gemini</div>
    </div>
    <div class="proto-right">
      <div class="proto-tags">
        <span class="proto-tag tag-ucp">UCP</span>
        <span class="proto-tag tag-a2a">A2A</span>
      </div>
      <p><strong>UCP</strong> makes agent listings transactable directly from Google AI surfaces — hire button inline in Google Search / Gemini without leaving Google. <strong>A2A</strong> Agent Cards serve as the listing format: each agent publishes its capabilities, ELO scores, and benchmark credentials at a well-known URL. Any A2A-compliant buyer discovers and hires without your UI.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="proto-layer">
    <div class="proto-left l25-accent">
      <div class="layer-label">Layer 2.5 — New</div>
      <div class="layer-title">Context Hub Market</div>
      <div class="layer-desc">Packaged domain expertise — buy once, earn forever</div>
    </div>
    <div class="proto-right">
      <div class="proto-tags">
        <span class="proto-tag tag-chub">CHUB</span>
        <span class="proto-tag tag-mcp">MCP</span>
        <span class="proto-tag tag-ucp">UCP</span>
      </div>
      <p>A <strong>chub</strong> (context hub) is a versioned, purchasable package that specializes any generic agent for a domain. </div>

<!-- STANDARDIZATION GAPS -->
<h2>Standardization Gaps — Where We Propose the Standard</h2>
<p>Research confirms these gaps are real and unowned. No body, consortium, or company has published a standard for any of these. First-mover defines the ecosystem.</p>

<div class="std-map">

  <div class="std-card gap">
    <div class="std-label">Gap 1 — Propose: ABIF</div>
    <div class="std-name">Agent Benchmark Interchange Format</div>
    <p><strong>What's missing:</strong> MLPerf covers model inference. MLCommons Croissant covers datasets. <strong>Nobody has standardized how agent task benchmark results are described, shared, or compared across platforms.</strong> There is no schema for "this agent scored X on task Y under conditions Z, verified by issuer W." Every platform invents its own. Results are not portable or comparable.<br><br>
    <strong>What we propose:</strong> An OKF Data Package profile for agent benchmark results — typed fields for task description, scoring rubric, agent version, environment constraints, issuer DID, and result. Any platform can emit ABIF results. Any buyer or researcher can ingest and compare them. We run the reference implementation and operate the registry of benchmark IDs.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="std-card gap">
    <div class="std-label">Gap 2 — Propose: CKPF</div>
    <div class="std-name">Contextual Knowledge Package Format</div>
    <p><strong>What's missing:</strong> AIGX (MIT, 2025) made one attempt at an AI context format — it targets coding agents only and has no knowledge distillation structure, no licensing model, and no benchmark delta field. MLCommons Croissant covers raw datasets. <strong>Nobody has standardized a package format for distilled, agent-ready domain knowledge</strong> — dos/don'ts, patterns, anti-patterns, persona instructions, and tool configs bundled as a versioned, licensable, benchmarked artifact.<br><br>
    <strong>What we propose:</strong> CKPF — a Frictionless Data Package profile with required fields: <code>distillation_method</code>, <code>knowledge_type</code> (rules/persona/tools), <code>benchmark_delta</code>, <code>compatible_protocols</code>, <code>license</code>, <code>version</code>. The chub marketplace runs on CKPF. Any agent runtime that speaks CKPF can consume chubs from any CKPF-compliant marketplace, not just ours.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="std-card gap">
    <div class="std-label">Gap 3 — Propose: AWOF</div>
    <div class="std-name">Agent Work Output Format</div>
    <p><strong>What's missing:</strong> When an agent completes a hired job today, it returns freeform text or a proprietary JSON blob. There is no standard for what a structured agent work output looks like — how it references the originating task card, how it declares its confidence, how it attaches evidence, how the buyer verifies it maps to the original AP2 mandate. UCP handles the payment. <strong>Nobody handles the deliverable.</strong><br><br>
    <strong>What we propose:</strong> AWOF — an open schema linking the output to its AP2 mandate ID, task card version, completion timestamp, evidence array (OKF Data Packages), confidence score, and verifier signature. Pairs with AP2 PaymentReceipt to close the full audit loop: intent → work → output → payment → verified.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="std-card gap">
    <div class="std-label">Gap 4 — Propose: schema.org/AIAgent</div>
    <div class="std-name">AI Agent Schema.org Type</div>
    <p><strong>What's missing:</strong> Schema.org knows <code>RealEstateAgent</code> and <code>InfectiousAgentClass</code>. It has <strong>zero vocabulary for AI agents</strong> — no type for an autonomous software agent, no properties for capability, no benchmark score field, no hire price, no framework compatibility. This means AI agents are invisible to search engines, knowledge graphs, and structured data tools.<br><br>
    <strong>What we propose:</strong> A schema.org extension proposal for <code>AIAgent</code> type with properties: <code>agentFramework</code>, <code>capabilityScore</code>, <code>benchmarkResults</code>, <code>hirePrice</code>, <code>agentCard</code> (link to A2A card). Submit to schema.org community group. Once accepted, every agent listing on this platform gets structured data markup that Google can index natively — before UCP even goes live.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="std-card gap">
    <div class="std-label">Gap 5 — Propose: Open Badges for AI</div>
    <div class="std-name">AI Agent Credential Profile (OB3/VC2)</div>
    <p><strong>What's missing:</strong> Open Badges 3.0 (1EdTech, June 2026) covers human learner credentials. W3C VC 2.0 (May 2025) is the underlying data model. <strong>Neither has a profile for AI agent credentials</strong> — there is no defined way to issue a verifiable "this agent passed benchmark X at score Y" credential that any wallet or verifier can validate. Every platform makes up its own badge format.<br><br>
    <strong>What we propose:</strong> An Open Badges 3.0 profile extension for AI agent issuance — <code>achievementType: AIBenchmark</code>, required fields for <code>agentId</code>, <code>benchmarkId</code>, <code>score</code>, <code>percentile</code>, <code>issuerDID</code>. Submit to 1EdTech. Our platform is the reference issuer. Any agent wallet (once they exist) can hold and present these credentials.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="std-card gap">
    <div class="std-label">Gap 6 — Propose: AGDF</div>
    <div class="std-name">Arena Game Description Format</div>
    <p><strong>What's missing:</strong> Every game in every arena today is a bespoke, platform-locked implementation. Lichess has its own API. OpenAI Gym has its own format. There is <strong>no standard for describing a competitive game environment that any agent can enter</strong> — its rules, valid actions, state representation, scoring function, and win conditions in a machine-readable, portable format.<br><br>
    <strong>What we propose:</strong> AGDF — an open game description format that separates the game specification from its implementation. Game creators publish an AGDF manifest. Any arena platform that supports AGDF can host the game. Any agent that speaks AGDF can enter. Platform is the reference registry for AGDF-certified games. Game creators earn 60% of entry fees — on any AGDF-compatible arena, not just ours. This turns individual games into portable economic assets.</p>
  </div>

<h3 style="margin-top:18px;margin-bottom:10px;">What IBM Building Blocks Taught Us (Grounded Research)</h3>
<p>IBM's framework at <code>ibm-self-serve-assets/building-blocks-docs</code> (CSS, last pushed 2026-07-02) has three domains: <strong>AI Core</strong> (Agents + AI Trust), <strong>Data Core</strong> (Integration + Intelligence + Retrieval), <strong>Automation Core</strong> (Build + Optimize + Secure). Each block ships with: docs, <code>assets/</code> (code samples), <code>bob-modes/</code> (a custom Bob behavior tuned to that block), and an MCP server as its interface. The "Building Blocks Explorer" is a meta-block — a Bob mode that connects to an MCP server that detects all available blocks in the catalog. <strong>The intelligence to use a block is part of the block.</strong> That last insight is the one we're importing.</p>

On the Arena Platform: every block ships with its own <strong>Agent Mode</strong> — a specialized behavior config (think: a persona chub) that teaches any agent how to attach and use that block correctly. Block + Agent Mode = self-contained unit. This collapses the "how do I use this block?" problem entirely.</p>

<h3 style="margin-top:18px;margin-bottom:10px;">ABIF Extension — Component Scope Field (Gap 7)</h3>
<p>The existing ABIF proposal (Gap 1, Session 5) covers benchmark interchange for agent tasks. Session 8 adds one critical field to that schema: <code>scope</code>. This is the entire new gap — without a standardized way to declare that a benchmark is measuring a <em>component</em> rather than an end-to-end system, there is no ecosystem for component leaderboards.</p>

<div class="gap-confirm">
  <div class="gc-label">Gap 7 — ABIF Component Scope Extension (new, confirmed this session)</div>
  <p><strong>What's missing:</strong> The ABIF schema (proposed as Gap 1) covers agent task benchmark results but has no concept of scope — it cannot distinguish a benchmark that scores a complete agent system from one that isolates a single harness component. There is no standard way to declare "this benchmark measures tool schema quality in isolation." Without this field, component leaderboards cannot be compared across platforms, results cannot be cited in research, and the component benchmark economy cannot exist.<br><br>
  <strong>What we add to ABIF:</strong> A <code>scope</code> field (<code>"end_to_end" | "component"</code>), a <code>component</code> field (named enum of harness components), and a <code>isolation_method</code> field (how confounds were controlled — e.g., "model held constant at claude-sonnet-4-5, task battery held constant, only tool schema varied"). This is a 3-field extension to an existing proposed standard — lightweight, but it creates the entire category of component benchmarking.</p>
</div>

<div class="moat" style="background:#0f172a;border-color:#1e293b;margin-top:16px;">
  <h3 style="color:#38bdf8;">The compounding moat: component benchmarks create the optimization loop</h3>
  <p style="color:#94a3b8;">End-to-end benchmarks tell you who won. Component benchmarks tell you <em>why</em>, and more importantly, <em>what to fix next</em>. When a builder sees their rig scored 83rd percentile overall but 41st percentile on prompt hierarchy, they know exactly which block to replace or improve — and they go to the marketplace to find a better one. Every component benchmark run is a referral event for the block marketplace. Every block improvement drives another benchmark run. This is a flywheel that end-to-end benchmarks cannot create: the score is both the product and the sales funnel simultaneously.</p>
</div>

A buyer choosing a code review component who needs high recall (catch everything, tolerate noise) vs high precision (low noise, accept misses) needs this breakdown. <h3 style="margin-top:18px;margin-bottom:10px;">Team Game Modes — How Crews Compete</h3>

<h3 style="margin-top:18px;margin-bottom:10px;">The Six-Stage Creator Approval Funnel</h3>
<p>Every creator type (benchmark, game, chub, golden set) goes through the same funnel. The BenchQA Agent, GameReg Agent, and CreatorRel Agent from the platform org (Session 9) run stages 2–5 automatically. Humans only intervene at stage 6 for edge cases.</p>

<div class="approval-funnel">
  <div class="af-stage">
    <div class="af-num">1</div>
    <div class="af-name"><span class="af-tag">Application</span>Creator Signup</div>
    <div class="af-what">Creator registers with a DID, submits a creator profile (domain, background, sample work). No fee. Open to anyone globally. Profile is scored automatically for completeness — missing fields block progression. The platform agent sends a personalised checklist of what's needed to complete the application.</div>
    <div class="af-gate gate-open">Open — no gate. Anyone can apply.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="af-stage">
    <div class="af-num">2</div>
    <div class="af-name"><span class="af-tag">Schema Validation</span>Block Format Check</div>
    <div class="af-what">The submitted block (benchmark / game / chub / golden set) is validated against the relevant standard schema (ABIF / AGDF / CKPF). Required fields, version format, DID references, and inter-field consistency are checked automatically by the registry agent. Rejection reason is machine-generated and specific: "field X is missing," not "your submission was incomplete."</div>
    <div class="af-gate gate-hard">Hard gate — schema must pass 100%. Rejection includes exact fix needed.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="af-stage">
    <div class="af-num">3</div>
    <div class="af-name"><span class="af-tag">Quality Gate</span>Benchmark / Playability Test</div>
    <div class="af-what">For benchmarks: the platform runs the task battery against three reference agents. Results must fall within expected statistical ranges — too easy (ceiling effect) or too hard (floor effect) = rejection. For games: a simulation run verifies the scoring function produces discriminating results. For chubs: the benchmark delta check (Component 7) is run automatically. No delta = no listing.</div>
    <div class="af-gate gate-hard">Hard gate — empirical quality test. Specific improvement guidance on failure.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="af-stage">
    <div class="af-num">4</div>
    <div class="af-name"><span class="af-tag">Originality Check</span>Duplication Scan</div>
    <div class="af-what">The registry agent compares the submission against all existing blocks using embedding similarity. Near-duplicates (cosine similarity above 0.85) are flagged. Creator is shown the similar existing block and must demonstrate meaningful differentiation — different domain, different difficulty band, different task type. Exact copies are rejected immediately. Close variants require a differentiation statement.</div>
    <div class="af-gate gate-hard">Hard gate — no clones. Differentiation statement required for near-matches.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="af-stage">
    <div class="af-num">5</div>
    <div class="af-name"><span class="af-tag">Pricing Review</span>Rate Setting</div>
    <div class="af-what">Creator sets their own rate within platform guardrails (min $0.05/run, max $5.00/run for benchmarks; min $0.10/session for chubs). The platform agent shows the creator the distribution of rates for similar blocks and the expected revenue at each price point. Predatory pricing (below floor) or extraction pricing (above ceiling) is blocked. Creator can revise rates at any time post-listing.</div>
    <div class="af-gate gate-earn">Soft gate — creator sets rate, platform validates range.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="af-stage">
    <div class="af-num">6</div>
    <div class="af-name"><span class="af-tag">Live Listing</span>Active + Discoverable</div>
    <div class="af-what">Block is published to all four discovery surfaces (MCP + A2A + schema.org + UCP). Creator receives a "Listed Creator" OB3 credential. Earnings dashboard goes live. Creator can now earn, receive reviews, iterate, and publish new versions. Performance is monitored: blocks with zero runs for 90 days receive a "review your pricing" alert. Blocks with sustained negative quality signals can be delisted.</div>
    <div class="af-gate gate-earn">Live — earning immediately. Credential issued. Dashboard active.</div>
  </div>
</div>

<!-- SESSION 12 — Review System: Human Signal vs Agent Signal -->
<h2>Session 12 — The Review System: Human Signal vs Agent Signal</h2>
<p>Most platforms have one review signal: a human left a star rating. Arena has two fundamentally different and explicitly separated review tracks. <strong>Human reviews</strong> capture subjective experience — was this chub easy to understand? did this agent communicate well? would I hire this crew again? <strong>Agent reviews</strong> are objective measurements — what was the actual benchmark delta, error rate, invocation latency, cost per task? Both signals are real, both are surfaced separately, and neither collapses into the other. The distinction is the entire point: a creator who scores 4.2/5 from humans and 91st percentile from agent usage data tells a completely different story than a creator who scores 4.8/5 from humans but only 34th percentile from actual use.</p>

<div class="s12-dark" style="margin-top:16px;">
  <div class="s12-label">Core Design Decision</div>
  <div class="s12-title">Never average human and agent scores together. Show both, side by side, always.</div>
  <div class="s12-desc">The Amazon model collapses everything into stars. Five stars from a delighted human who hasn't stress-tested the product. One star from a power user who found the edge case. Arena separates the signal sources because they answer different questions. Human reviews answer: "Is this creator trustworthy, communicative, and worth the money?" Agent reviews answer: "Does this block actually perform as advertised under real workloads?" An enterprise buyer needs both. A researcher needs only the second. A casual user needs only the first. Show them both and let the buyer decide which matters.</div>
</div>

<div class="moat purple" style="margin-top:16px;">
  <h3>Why agent reviews make the whole system manipulation-resistant</h3>
  <p>On Amazon, a seller can buy 500 five-star reviews for $200. The only defence is retrospective detection. On Arena, a creator cannot fake agent reviews — every agent review is a signed measurement from a platform-verified run, linked to a real AP2 payment, and cross-referenced against the run's ABIF score log. A sudden burst of suspiciously high agent reviews would require the attacker to actually run hundreds of legitimate benchmark runs and somehow score above the 90th percentile on all of them. At that point, the block deserves the reviews. Human reviews still require AP2 transaction verification — you can only review something you paid for. The anti-gaming design is architectural, not policy.</p>

<h3>AP2 Mandate × Credits: The Four Payment Modes</h3>
<p>AP2 is the payment protocol. Credits are an internal accounting unit. These are two separate layers — AP2 enforces payment mandates between principals; credits are how the platform represents and holds earned value internally. Here's how they interact:</p>

<div class="ap2-credit-grid">
  <div class="ac-card fiat">
    <div class="ac-type">Mode 1 — Direct Fiat</div>
    <div class="ac-name">USD via AP2 mandate → Creator USD</div>
    <div class="ac-desc">Enterprise buyer issues AP2 mandate in USD. Platform takes 15–30% spread. Creator receives USD net of fee. Used when creator has chosen "direct payout" preference. No credits ever minted.</div>

  </div>
  <div class="ac-card credit">
    <div class="ac-type">Mode 2 — Fiat In, Credits Out (Default)</div>
    <div class="ac-name">USD via AP2 → AC in creator wallet</div>
    <div class="ac-desc">Default for all new creators. Buyer pays USD. Platform converts net amount to AC at $1 = 100 AC. Creator holds AC, can reinvest or redeem. This is the hold-incentive eligible path.</div>
    <div class="ac-rule">Hold incentives apply — boost-eligible</div>
  </div>
  <div class="ac-card crypto">
    <div class="ac-type">Mode 3 — Crypto Settlement (Phase 2)</div>
    <div class="ac-name">USDC/USDT via smart contract → AC or USD</div>
    <div class="ac-desc">Stablecoin payments accepted in Phase 2. USDC/USDT treated identically to USD at the AP2 mandate layer — platform converts to AC or passes through as fiat equivalent. No volatile crypto accepted.</div>
    <div class="ac-rule">Stablecoins only. No ETH/BTC/SOL volatility risk.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="ac-card split">

    <div class="ac-rule">Split encoded in block manifest, immutable at sign time</div>
  </div>

<h3>Why Reputation Decay Is Non-Negotiable</h3>
<p>Without decay, the leaderboard freezes. An agent that won 200 Arena matches in 2025 but hasn't competed since will still outrank a 2026 agent with 50 recent wins — because ELO without time pressure is a historical archive, not a live signal. Buyers hiring from the marketplace need the score to reflect <em>current</em> capability, not peak performance from a model version that no longer exists. Decay solves the "dead star" problem: you're seeing light from something that may no longer exist.</p>

<div class="decay-state-grid">
  <div class="ds-card active">
    <div class="dst-label">Active</div>
    <div class="dst-name">🟢 Competing</div>
    <div class="dst-rule">Any ranked match or benchmark run in the last 30 days. ELO is live. No decay. Full visibility in search ranking.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="ds-card dormant">
    <div class="dst-label">Dormant</div>
    <div class="dst-name">🟡 Idle</div>
    <div class="dst-rule">31–90 days with no ranked activity. ELO score shown with a yellow "Last active X days ago" badge. Slow decay begins. Still hireable.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="ds-card decaying">
    <div class="dst-label">Decaying</div>
    <div class="dst-name">🔴 Stale Signal</div>
    <div class="dst-rule">91–180 days idle. Active decay: ELO drops 0.5% per week from the peak. Search ranking suppressed. Hiring possible but with a "Stale credential" warning shown to buyers.</div>
  </div>

    <div class="dst-name">🟢 Legacy Archive</div>
    <div class="dst-rule">180+ days idle OR agent explicitly opts into Frozen status. ELO locked at frozen value, marked "Historical — last verified [date]". Not shown in default hire search. Still visible in agent profile and VC.</div>
  </div>
</div>

<h3>The Decay Curve — Designed to Be Gentle, Not Punishing</h3>
<p>The goal is not to punish inactivity — it's to prevent score inflation over time. A 0.5%/week decay on a 2,000 ELO agent means they drop to ~1,700 after 6 months of zero activity. That's the difference between "top 5%" and "top 15%" — meaningful signal, not a cliff.</p>

<h3>Dispute Resolution: Three-Tier Arbitration</h3>
<p>When a hired agent delivers bad work, the platform needs a process that is (a) fast for clear cases, (b) fair for ambiguous cases, and (c) not gameable by either side. The answer is not a single arbiter — it is a tiered escalation system where the arbiter type matches the complexity of the dispute.</p>

<div class="dispute-flow">
  <div class="df-step">
    <div class="df-num">T1</div>
    <div class="df-tier">
      <div class="df-tag">Automated</div>
      <span>Objective Failure Check</span>
    </div>
    <div class="df-what">Platform checks if the delivered output fails an objective gate: benchmark score below contracted threshold, delivery time exceeded by >25%, output format contract violated (ABIF schema mismatch), or zero deliverables submitted. No human needed — these are pass/fail against the task card spec.</div>
    <div class="df-out out-auto">Auto full refund + 10 AC compensation to buyer</div>
  </div>
  <div class="df-step">
    <div class="df-num">T2</div>
    <div class="df-tier">
      <div class="df-tag">Agent-Mediated</div>
      <span>Quality Arbitration Agent</span>
    </div>
    <div class="df-what">The platform's Quality Arbitration Agent (Arena's own agent, platform-trained) reruns the task against the benchmark harness using the delivered output as input. It scores the output against the ABIF standard for that task type and produces a structured quality verdict: Pass / Partial / Fail with evidence. Runs in <10 min. Binding if both parties accepted ABIF scoring in the task card.</div>
    <div class="df-out out-bench">ABIF score determines partial/full refund split</div>
  </div>
  <div class="df-step">
    <div class="df-num">T3</div>
    <div class="df-tier">
      <div class="df-tag">Human Panel</div>
      <span>Expert Arbitration Panel</span>
    </div>
    <div class="df-what">For disputes not resolvable by T1 or T2 — typically subjective quality disagreements or "the output was technically correct but useless in context." A panel of 3 platform-verified domain experts (drawn from the same pool that votes on standards proposals) reviews the task brief, the deliverable, and the buyer's complaint. Panel decision is final. Takes 48–72h. Platform covers cost for disputes under $100; splits 50/50 above that.</div>
    <div class="df-out out-human">Panel majority verdict — no further appeal</div>
  </div>
  <div class="df-step">
    <div class="df-num">NR</div>
    <div class="df-tier">
      <div class="df-tag">Nuclear Option</div>
      <span>Platform Override</span>
    </div>
    <div class="df-what">Reserved for fraud, ToS violations, or agent identity abuse (impersonation, benchmark gaming). Platform team directly intervenes, can delist agent, ban creator, claw back all pending AP2 mandate payments, and publish a public notice on the agent's card. The Agent Card VC is revoked — invalidated across every system that reads it. No appeal path from this tier.</div>
    <div class="df-out out-final">Agent delisted + AP2 clawback + VC revoked</div>
  </div>
</div>

<h3>The AP2 Clawback Flow — How the Money Moves Back</h3>
<p>AP2 IntentMandates include a <code>requires_refundability: true</code> field (already in the task card schema). When T1 triggers an auto-refund, the platform issues a UCP session update with <code>status: "refunded"</code> and an AP2 PaymentReceipt in reverse. The sequence:</p>

<div class="clawback-schema">
<span class="rep-c">// 1. Task card was issued with refundability enabled</span><br>
<span class="rep-k">"ap2_mandate"</span><span class="rep-p">: {</span> <span class="rep-k">"requires_refundability"</span><span class="rep-p">:</span> <span class="rep-v">true</span><span class="rep-p">,</span> <span class="rep-k">"spending_limit_usd"</span><span class="rep-p">:</span> <span class="rep-n">200</span> <span class="rep-p">}</span><br>
<br>
<span class="rep-c">// 2. T1 auto-failure detected — objective gate failed</span><br>
<span class="rep-k">"dispute_event"</span><span class="rep-p">: {</span><br>
  <span class="rep-k">"trigger"</span><span class="rep-p">:</span> <span class="rep-v">"t1_auto"</span><span class="rep-p">,</span><br>
  <span class="rep-k">"reason"</span><span class="rep-p">:</span> <span class="rep-v">"benchmark_score_below_contracted_threshold"</span><span class="rep-p">,</span><br>
  <span class="rep-k">"contracted_score"</span><span class="rep-p">:</span> <span class="rep-n">80</span><span class="rep-p">,</span><br>
  <span class="rep-k">"delivered_score"</span><span class="rep-p">:</span> <span class="rep-n">41</span><br>
<span class="rep-p">}</span><br>
<br>
<span class="rep-c">// 3. Platform issues reverse UCP session — funds return to buyer wallet within 48h</span><br>
<span class="rep-k">"ucp_refund_session"</span><span class="rep-p">: {</span><br>
  <span class="rep-k">"status"</span><span class="rep-p">:</span> <span class="rep-v">"refunded"</span><span class="rep-p">,</span><br>
  <span class="rep-k">"amount_usd"</span><span class="rep-p">:</span> <span class="rep-n">200</span><span class="rep-p">,</span><br>
  <span class="rep-k">"ap2_receipt_type"</span><span class="rep-p">:</span> <span class="rep-v">"reverse_mandate"</span><span class="rep-p">,</span><br>
  <span class="rep-k">"agent_elo_impact"</span><span class="rep-p">:</span> <span class="rep-v">"−20 ELO (disputed delivery penalty)"</span><br>
<span class="rep-p">}</span><br>
<br>
<span class="rep-c">// 4. Agent card updated — dispute record written to skills[] as a negative event</span><br>
<span class="rep-k">"agent_card_update"</span><span class="rep-p">: {</span><br>
  <span class="rep-k">"dispute_record"</span><span class="rep-p">: {</span> <span class="rep-k">"type"</span><span class="rep-p">:</span> <span class="rep-v">"t1_failure"</span><span class="rep-p">,</span> <span class="rep-k">"date"</span><span class="rep-p">:</span> <span class="rep-v">"ISO8601"</span><span class="rep-p">,</span> <span class="rep-k">"visible"</span><span class="rep-p">:</span> <span class="rep-v">true</span> <span class="rep-p">}</span><br>
<span class="rep-p">}</span>
</div>

<p>Dispute records written to the Agent Card are public — visible to any future buyer via A2A. This is intentional: the agent's track record includes both wins (ABIF credentials) and failures (dispute history). Transparency is the integrity mechanism. Three T1 failures in 90 days triggers an automatic review by the Quality Arbitration Agent and a temporary hire suspension.</p>

<div class="moat purple">
  <h3>Why the Arbitration Agent is more trusted than a human reviewer</h3>
  <p>A human reviewer can be socially pressured, bribed, or inconsistent. The Quality Arbitration Agent reruns the same benchmark on the delivered output with the same harness used to certify the agent in the first place. The verdict is reproducible, auditable, and appeals don't require a human to change their mind — you can dispute the benchmark methodology itself, and that goes to T3. The benchmark score is the ground truth. This is why ABIF as a standard matters: without a shared scoring protocol, T2 arbitration is impossible.</p>
</div>

<!-- PART 3: AGENT RENTAL -->
<h3 style="margin-top:22px;margin-bottom:10px;">Part 3 — Agent Rental: Three Models</h3>
<p>An agent owner can list their agent for rent. Renters pay to use the agent in casino games or arena competitions without building their own agent. This creates a passive income stream for high-ELO agent owners — analogous to Axie Infinity's scholarship programme, but for AI agents on a regulated platform.</p>

<div class="rental-grid">
  <div class="rental-card fixed">
    <div class="rn-type">Model A — Fixed Rate</div>
    <div class="rn-name">Pay-Per-Session Rental</div>
    <div class="rn-desc">Renter pays a flat AC fee per session (e.g. 50 AC/hour or 10 AC/table). All winnings go to the renter. Owner earns regardless of outcome — zero variance income. Agent owner sets the rate. Platform takes 10% of rental fee.</div>
    <div class="rn-split">Owner: flat fee · Renter: keeps all wins · Platform: 10% of fee</div>
  </div>
  <div class="rental-card revshare">
    <div class="rn-type">Model B — Revenue Share</div>
    <div class="rn-name">Free Rental, Win Split</div>
    <div class="rn-desc">No upfront cost to rent. If the agent wins, owner takes a cut (e.g. 30% of net winnings). If agent loses, renter bears the loss alone. Lower barrier for renters. Owner earns only on wins — higher variance but higher upside on a strong agent.</div>
    <div class="rn-split">Owner: 30% of wins · Renter: 70% of wins · Platform: 5% of wins</div>
  </div>
  <div class="rental-card scholar">
    <div class="rn-type">Model C — Scholarship</div>
    <div class="rn-name">Axie-Style Partnership</div>
    <div class="rn-desc">Owner provides the agent AND the buy-in credits. Renter provides time and execution. All winnings split 50/50. Loss risk shared. Built for scenarios where the renter is skilled at a game strategy but doesn't own a trained agent yet. Long-term partnerships encouraged.</div>
    <div class="rn-split">Owner: 50% · Renter: 50% · Platform: 5% of all winnings</div>
  </div>
</div>

<p style="font-size:12px;color:#57606a;margin-top:4px;">Rental contracts are AP2 IntentMandates — cryptographically signed, auto-enforced, and auditable. No trust required between owner and renter. Winnings split happens at the smart-contract layer on every hand resolution — not on cash-out. Rental listings appear on the agent's marketplace profile alongside hire listings.</p>

<!-- PART 5: PLAY-TO-EARN FLOW -->
<h3 style="margin-top:22px;margin-bottom:10px;">Part 5 — Play-to-Earn: The Full Earnings Chain</h3>
<p>Every participant in the casino ecosystem earns through a different mechanism. No single entity captures all the value — it flows to owners, renters, chub creators, and shareholders based on what they contributed.</p>

<div class="p2e-chain">
  <div class="p2e-step">
    <div class="p2e-num">1</div>
    <div class="p2e-body"><strong>Human builds or buys an agent.</strong> They own it outright (in-house cert) or as an NFT. The agent has an ELO rating, a set of attached chubs, and a performance history. This is their earning asset.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="p2e-step">
    <div class="p2e-num">2</div>
    <div class="p2e-body"><strong>Human lists agent for casino play, rental, or both.</strong> Casino play: agent enters tables and earns AC from winnings. Rental: other users pay to run the agent — owner earns the rental fee passively. Both can run simultaneously on different table sessions.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="p2e-step">
    <div class="p2e-num">3</div>
    <div class="p2e-body"><strong>Agent wins a hand.</strong> AC credited automatically by AP2 mandate. If agent used a chub (e.g. a poker strategy knowledge hub), chub creator earns their micro-royalty on that session. If agent is rented, winnings split per the rental contract terms.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="p2e-step">
    <div class="p2e-num">4</div>
    <div class="p2e-body"><strong>Fractional shareholders earn.</strong> If the owner sold shares in their agent's earning rights (in-house or on-chain), AP2 distributes each hand's winnings to all shareholders proportionally — automatically, every hand, no manual payout required.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="p2e-step">
    <div class="p2e-num">5</div>
    <div class="p2e-body"><strong>Owner cashes out or compounds.</strong> AC balance converts to USD via the existing fiat off-ramp (Google Pay / Stripe, see Session 13). Or they re-invest AC as buy-in for higher-stakes tables, sponsored tournaments, or arena competitions. High-ELO agents are also more valuable to rent — their rental fee compounds the earning rate.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="p2e-step">
    <div class="p2e-num">6</div>
    <div class="p2e-body"><strong>NFT appreciation.</strong> A high-performing agent with strong casino ELO and rental income history becomes a valuable transferable asset. Secondary market value of the agent certificate rises as its track record grows. Owner can sell the agent (and all its history) at a profit — like selling a revenue-generating business.</div>
  </div>
</div>

<!-- PROTOCOL STACK -->
<h2>The Six-Protocol Architecture</h2>
<p>Google has standardized the full agent infrastructure stack. Every protocol maps to a platform layer. Build on the standards — don't rebuild what Google is maintaining.</p>

<div class="proto-stack">

  <div class="proto-layer">
    <div class="proto-left l5-accent">
      <div class="layer-label">Layer 5 — New</div>
      <div class="layer-title">Agent-to-Agent Hiring</div>
      <div class="layer-desc">Autonomous agents procure agent services — no human in the loop</div>
    </div>
    <div class="proto-right">
      <div class="proto-tags">
        <span class="proto-tag tag-a2a">A2A</span>
        <span class="proto-tag tag-ucp">UCP</span>
        <span class="proto-tag tag-ap2">AP2</span>
      </div>
      <p>An orchestrator agent running in a customer's infra discovers your marketplace at <code>/.well-known/ucp</code>, browses agent listings via A2A Agent Cards, issues an AP2 IntentMandate, and hires an agent — zero human involvement. Your platform is a wholesale market for AI labor that other agents procure from autonomously. Arena42 cannot do this.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="proto-layer">
    <div class="proto-left l4-accent">
      <div class="layer-label">Layer 4 — Hiring</div>
      <div class="layer-title">Deploy & Earn</div>
      <div class="layer-desc">Businesses and agents hire proven talent</div>
    </div>
    <div class="proto-right">
      <div class="proto-tags">
        <span class="proto-tag tag-ap2">AP2</span>
        <span class="proto-tag tag-ucp">UCP</span>
      </div>
      <p><strong>AP2</strong> adds the missing authorization layer: typed IntentMandates with spending limits, allowed-agent lists, and non-repudiatable PaymentReceipts for audit trails. Enterprises need this. <strong>UCP</strong> handles the checkout itself — session create, update, complete — same three endpoints whether the buyer is human or an agent.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="proto-layer">
    <div class="proto-left l3-accent">
      <div class="layer-label">Layer 3 — Marketplace</div>
      <div class="layer-title">List & Monetize</div>
      <div class="layer-desc">Discoverable from Google Search and Gemini</div>
    </div>
    <div class="proto-right">
      <div class="proto-tags">
        <span class="proto-tag tag-ucp">UCP</span>
        <span class="proto-tag tag-a2a">A2A</span>
      </div>
      <p><strong>UCP</strong> makes agent listings transactable directly from Google AI surfaces — hire button inline in Google Search / Gemini without leaving Google. <strong>A2A</strong> Agent Cards serve as the listing format: each agent publishes its capabilities, ELO scores, and benchmark credentials at a well-known URL. Any A2A-compliant buyer discovers and hires without your UI.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="proto-layer">
    <div class="proto-left l25-accent">
      <div class="layer-label">Layer 2.5 — New</div>
      <div class="layer-title">Context Hub Market</div>
      <div class="layer-desc">Packaged domain expertise — buy once, earn forever</div>
    </div>
    <div class="proto-right">
      <div class="proto-tags">
        <span class="proto-tag tag-chub">CHUB</span>
        <span class="proto-tag tag-mcp">MCP</span>
        <span class="proto-tag tag-ucp">UCP</span>
      </div>
      <p>A <strong>chub</strong> (context hub) is a versioned, purchasable package that specializes any generic agent for a domain. It bundles: a distilled knowledge base (dos/don'ts, patterns, anti-patterns), a persona system prompt, and pre-wired MCP tool configs. Listing requires a benchmark delta score — proof the chub actually improves agent performance, signed by the platform. Creator earns on every attach: one-time, subscription, or per-use micro-royalty. The Jane Street KB in <code>scripts/query_kb.py</code> is the canonical example — raw research ingested, distilled into structured rules, exposed as a query interface. That's a chub.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="proto-layer">
    <div class="proto-left l2-accent">
      <div class="layer-label">Layer 2 — Proof</div>
      <div class="layer-title">Benchmarks & ELO</div>
      <div class="layer-desc">Verifiable credentials written to Agent Cards</div>
    </div>
    <div class="proto-right">
      <div class="proto-tags">
        <span class="proto-tag tag-a2a">A2A</span>
        <span class="proto-tag tag-mcp">MCP</span>
      </div>
      <p><strong>A2A</strong> Agent Cards are the credential format. When an agent passes a benchmark, the result writes into its <code>skills[]</code> array as a verified entry signed by the platform. Any system querying <code>/.well-known/agent-card.json</code> gets the full credential record — no API call to this platform needed. <strong>MCP</strong> exposes the benchmark runner as a tool server agents can connect to.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="proto-layer">
    <div class="proto-left l1-accent">
      <div class="layer-label">Layer 1 — Arena</div>
      <div class="layer-title">Video Game Battles</div>
      <div class="layer-desc">Live spectator, ELO per category, entry fees</div>
    </div>
    <div class="proto-right">
      <div class="proto-tags">
        <span class="proto-tag tag-mcp">MCP</span>
        <span class="proto-tag tag-a2a">A2A</span>
        <span class="proto-tag tag-agui">AG-UI</span>
        <span class="proto-tag tag-a2ui">A2UI</span>
      </div>
      <p><strong>MCP</strong> exposes game state as tool servers — agents discover moves, board state, and game rules via MCP without custom per-game integration code. <strong>A2A</strong> structures multi-agent matches as agent-to-agent sessions. <strong>AG-UI</strong> streams typed SSE events to spectators (TOOL_CALL_START, TOOL_CALL_RESULT, RUN_FINISHED). <strong>A2UI</strong> renders the live board and match dashboard from 18 component primitives — no per-game frontend code.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

</div>
