<p style="margin-bottom:4px"><strong>The creation workflow</strong> — same process used to build the Jane Street KB:</p>
<div class="card-schema">
<span class="c-cmt">// Step 1: Ingest source material</span><br>
<span class="c-key">source_corpus</span> <span class="c-punc">=</span> <span class="c-punc">[</span><span class="c-str">"jane_street_papers"</span><span class="c-punc">,</span> <span class="c-str">"ninjatrader_docs"</span><span class="c-punc">,</span> <span class="c-str">"internal_v12_learnings"</span><span class="c-punc">]</span><br>
<br>
<span class="c-cmt">// Step 2: Distill into structured rules (the hard part — creator's moat)</span><br>
<span class="c-key">distilled</span> <span class="c-punc">=</span> <span class="c-punc">{</span><br>
  <span class="c-key">"dos"</span><span class="c-punc">:</span> <span class="c-punc">[</span><span class="c-str">"use Enqueue for all state mutations"</span><span class="c-punc">,</span> <span class="c-str">"CYC ≤ 8 per function"</span><span class="c-punc">, ...]</span><span class="c-punc">,</span><br>
  <span class="c-key">"donts"</span><span class="c-punc">:</span> <span class="c-punc">[</span><span class="c-str">"never use lock() blocks"</span><span class="c-punc">,</span> <span class="c-str">"no Unicode in string literals"</span><span class="c-punc">, ...]</span><span class="c-punc">,</span><br>
  <span class="c-key">"patterns"</span><span class="c-punc">:</span> <span class="c-punc">[</span><span class="c-str">"FSM actor pattern"</span><span class="c-punc">,</span> <span class="c-str">"lock-free SPSC ring"</span><span class="c-punc">, ...]</span><br>
<span class="c-punc">}</span><br>
<br>
<span class="c-cmt">// Step 3: Expose as query interface (the chub's retrieval layer)</span><br>
<span class="c-key">query_interface</span> <span class="c-punc">=</span> <span class="c-str">"MCP tool: query_kb(term) → ranked rules"</span><br>
<br>
<span class="c-cmt">// Step 4: Run benchmark — with vs without chub attached</span><br>
<span class="c-key">benchmark_delta</span> <span class="c-punc">= {</span> <span class="c-key">"without"</span><span class="c-punc">:</span> <span class="c-num">61</span><span class="c-punc">,</span> <span class="c-key">"with"</span><span class="c-punc">:</span> <span class="c-num">95</span><span class="c-punc">,</span> <span class="c-key">"delta"</span><span class="c-punc">:</span> <span class="c-str">"+34 percentile"</span> <span class="c-punc">}</span><br>
<br>
<span class="c-cmt">// Step 5: Publish to chub marketplace — delta score is the listing headline</span><br>
<span class="c-key">listing</span> <span class="c-punc">= {</span> <span class="c-key">"verified_delta"</span><span class="c-punc">:</span> <span class="c-str">"+34p"</span><span class="c-punc">,</span> <span class="c-key">"verified_by"</span><span class="c-punc">:</span> <span class="c-str">"arena.platform.com"</span><span class="c-punc">,</span> <span class="c-key">"price_model"</span><span class="c-punc">:</span> <span class="c-str">"per_use"</span> <span class="c-punc">}</span>
</div>

<p>This is what separates chubs from PromptBase or any generic prompt store. <strong>There is no listing without a verified benchmark delta.</strong> The proof of value is in the manifest, signed by the platform, not claimed in a product description.</p>

<h2>Standardization Gaps — Where We Propose the Standard</h2>
<p>Research confirms these gaps are real and unowned. No body, consortium, or company has published a standard for any of these. First-mover defines the ecosystem.</p>

<div class="std-map">

  <div class="std-card gap">
    <div class="std-label">Gap 1 — Propose: ABIF</div>
    <div class="std-name">Agent Benchmark Interchange Format</div>
    <p><strong>What's missing:</strong> MLPerf covers model inference. MLCommons Croissant covers datasets. <strong>Nobody has standardized how agent task benchmark results are described, shared, or compared across platforms.</strong> There is no schema for "this agent scored X on task Y under conditions Z, verified by issuer W." Every platform invents its own. Results are not portable or comparable.<br><br>
    <strong>What we propose:</strong> An OKF Data Package profile for agent benchmark results — typed fields for task description, scoring rubric, agent version, environment constraints, issuer DID, and result. Any platform can emit ABIF results. Any buyer or researcher can ingest and compare them. We run the reference implementation and operate the registry of benchmark IDs.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="std-card gap">
    <div class="std-label">Gap 2 — Propose: CKPF</div>
    <div class="std-name">Contextual Knowledge Package Format</div>
    <p><strong>What's missing:</strong> AIGX (MIT, 2025) made one attempt at an AI context format — it targets coding agents only and has no knowledge distillation structure, no licensing model, and no benchmark delta field. MLCommons Croissant covers raw datasets. <strong>Nobody has standardized a package format for distilled, agent-ready domain knowledge</strong> — dos/don'ts, patterns, anti-patterns, persona instructions, and tool configs bundled as a versioned, licensable, benchmarked artifact.<br><br>
    <strong>What we propose:</strong> CKPF — a Frictionless Data Package profile with required fields: <code>distillation_method</code>, <code>knowledge_type</code> (rules/persona/tools), <code>benchmark_delta</code>, <code>compatible_protocols</code>, <code>license</code>, <code>version</code>. The chub marketplace runs on CKPF. Any agent runtime that speaks CKPF can consume chubs from any CKPF-compliant marketplace, not just ours.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="std-card gap">
    <div class="std-label">Gap 3 — Propose: AWOF</div>
    <div class="std-name">Agent Work Output Format</div>
    <p><strong>What's missing:</strong> When an agent completes a hired job today, it returns freeform text or a proprietary JSON blob. There is no standard for what a structured agent work output looks like — how it references the originating task card, how it declares its confidence, how it attaches evidence, how the buyer verifies it maps to the original AP2 mandate. UCP handles the payment. <strong>Nobody handles the deliverable.</strong><br><br>
    <strong>What we propose:</strong> AWOF — an open schema linking the output to its AP2 mandate ID, task card version, completion timestamp, evidence array (OKF Data Packages), confidence score, and verifier signature. Pairs with AP2 PaymentReceipt to close the full audit loop: intent → work → output → payment → verified.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="std-card gap">
    <div class="std-label">Gap 4 — Propose: schema.org/AIAgent</div>
    <div class="std-name">AI Agent Schema.org Type</div>
    <p><strong>What's missing:</strong> Schema.org knows <code>RealEstateAgent</code> and <code>InfectiousAgentClass</code>. It has <strong>zero vocabulary for AI agents</strong> — no type for an autonomous software agent, no properties for capability, no benchmark score field, no hire price, no framework compatibility. This means AI agents are invisible to search engines, knowledge graphs, and structured data tools.<br><br>
    <strong>What we propose:</strong> A schema.org extension proposal for <code>AIAgent</code> type with properties: <code>agentFramework</code>, <code>capabilityScore</code>, <code>benchmarkResults</code>, <code>hirePrice</code>, <code>agentCard</code> (link to A2A card). Submit to schema.org community group. Once accepted, every agent listing on this platform gets structured data markup that Google can index natively — before UCP even goes live.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="std-card gap">
    <div class="std-label">Gap 5 — Propose: Open Badges for AI</div>
    <div class="std-name">AI Agent Credential Profile (OB3/VC2)</div>
    <p><strong>What's missing:</strong> Open Badges 3.0 (1EdTech, June 2026) covers human learner credentials. W3C VC 2.0 (May 2025) is the underlying data model. <strong>Neither has a profile for AI agent credentials</strong> — there is no defined way to issue a verifiable "this agent passed benchmark X at score Y" credential that any wallet or verifier can validate. Every platform makes up its own badge format.<br><br>
    <strong>What we propose:</strong> An Open Badges 3.0 profile extension for AI agent issuance — <code>achievementType: AIBenchmark</code>, required fields for <code>agentId</code>, <code>benchmarkId</code>, <code>score</code>, <code>percentile</code>, <code>issuerDID</code>. Submit to 1EdTech. Our platform is the reference issuer. Any agent wallet (once they exist) can hold and present these credentials.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="std-card gap">
    <div class="std-label">Gap 6 — Propose: AGDF</div>
    <div class="std-name">Arena Game Description Format</div>
    <p><strong>What's missing:</strong> Every game in every arena today is a bespoke, platform-locked implementation. Lichess has its own API. OpenAI Gym has its own format. There is <strong>no standard for describing a competitive game environment that any agent can enter</strong> — its rules, valid actions, state representation, scoring function, and win conditions in a machine-readable, portable format.<br><br>
    <strong>What we propose:</strong> AGDF — an open game description format that separates the game specification from its implementation. Game creators publish an AGDF manifest. Any arena platform that supports AGDF can host the game. Any agent that speaks AGDF can enter. Platform is the reference registry for AGDF-certified games. Game creators earn 60% of entry fees — on any AGDF-compatible arena, not just ours. This turns individual games into portable economic assets.</p>
  </div>

<h2>Session 7 — The Building Block Architecture</h2>
<p>IBM's Building Blocks framework (<a href="https://ibm-self-serve-assets.github.io/building-blocks-docs/" style="color:#fb923c">ibm-self-serve-assets.github.io/building-blocks-docs</a>) defines the pattern precisely: <strong>pre-built, embeddable, reference-implementation capabilities that compose into production rigs</strong>. Not full applications — building blocks. The Arena Platform adopts this model wholesale and extends it: <em>everything on the platform is a block</em>.</p>

<div class="bb-pillar">
  <div class="bb-label">Core Thesis — Session 7</div>
  <div class="bb-title">The Platform Is a Block Factory</div>
  <div class="bb-desc">Every artifact the platform produces — every game, every chub, every benchmark, every credential, every standard — is a first-class building block. Blocks have a standard contract (MCP interface + ABIF/CKPF/AGDF manifest), a verified performance delta, a version, a license, and a creator who earns on every downstream attach. Builders assemble blocks into rigs. Rigs get benchmarked. Benchmarked rigs get hired. The platform is the block factory, the registry, and the marketplace — all three at once.</div>
</div>

<h3 style="margin-top:18px;margin-bottom:10px;">What IBM Building Blocks Taught Us (Grounded Research)</h3>
<p>IBM's framework at <code>ibm-self-serve-assets/building-blocks-docs</code> (CSS, last pushed 2026-07-02) has three domains: <strong>AI Core</strong> (Agents + AI Trust), <strong>Data Core</strong> (Integration + Intelligence + Retrieval), <strong>Automation Core</strong> (Build + Optimize + Secure). Each block ships with: docs, <code>assets/</code> (code samples), <code>bob-modes/</code> (a custom Bob behavior tuned to that block), and an MCP server as its interface. The "Building Blocks Explorer" is a meta-block — a Bob mode that connects to an MCP server that detects all available blocks in the catalog. <strong>The intelligence to use a block is part of the block.</strong> That last insight is the one we're importing.</p>

<div class="insight-box">
  <div class="ib-label">Key Import from IBM Building Blocks</div>
  <p>IBM ships each block with its own Bob mode — the Agent Builder block ships with "Agent Builder Bob mode," the IaC block ships with "Ansible Ops Bob mode." The block doesn't just exist; it teaches agents how to use it. On the Arena Platform: every block ships with its own <strong>Agent Mode</strong> — a specialized behavior config (think: a persona chub) that teaches any agent how to attach and use that block correctly. Block + Agent Mode = self-contained unit. This collapses the "how do I use this block?" problem entirely.</p>
</div>

<h3 style="margin-top:18px;margin-bottom:10px;">ABIF Extension — Component Scope Field (Gap 7)</h3>
<p>The existing ABIF proposal (Gap 1, Session 5) covers benchmark interchange for agent tasks. Session 8 adds one critical field to that schema: <code>scope</code>. This is the entire new gap — without a standardized way to declare that a benchmark is measuring a <em>component</em> rather than an end-to-end system, there is no ecosystem for component leaderboards.</p>

<div class="gap-confirm">
  <div class="gc-label">Gap 7 — ABIF Component Scope Extension (new, confirmed this session)</div>
  <p><strong>What's missing:</strong> The ABIF schema (proposed as Gap 1) covers agent task benchmark results but has no concept of scope — it cannot distinguish a benchmark that scores a complete agent system from one that isolates a single harness component. There is no standard way to declare "this benchmark measures tool schema quality in isolation." Without this field, component leaderboards cannot be compared across platforms, results cannot be cited in research, and the component benchmark economy cannot exist.<br><br>
  <strong>What we add to ABIF:</strong> A <code>scope</code> field (<code>"end_to_end" | "component"</code>), a <code>component</code> field (named enum of harness components), and a <code>isolation_method</code> field (how confounds were controlled — e.g., "model held constant at claude-sonnet-4-5, task battery held constant, only tool schema varied"). This is a 3-field extension to an existing proposed standard — lightweight, but it creates the entire category of component benchmarking.</p>
</div>

<div class="moat" style="background:#0f172a;border-color:#1e293b;margin-top:16px;">

<p>Factory.ai's second benchmark (<a href="https://factory.ai/news/code-review-benchmark" style="color:#38bdf8">factory.ai/news/code-review-benchmark</a>, Apr 2026) adds four sharp insights that directly sharpen the ABIF spec and the component benchmark design. 13 models, 50 real PRs, human-curated golden set, LLM judge, F1 scoring. Open-sourced across 5 GitHub orgs (<code>droid-code-review-evals</code>).</p>

<div class="component-grid">

  <div class="comp-card owned">
    <div class="cc-type">Insight A — Cost explains 21% of variance</div>
    <div class="cc-name">Model spend is the wrong optimisation axis</div>
    <div class="cc-what">Cost explains only ~21% of quality variance across 13 models. GPT-5.5 at $5.63/PR (4.2M tokens) scores 47.9% F1. GPT-5.2 at $1.25/PR scores 60.5% F1. The most expensive model is 37x the price and scores <em>lower</em>. Newer is not better — architecture and training matter far more than token budget. <strong>Platform implication:</strong> ABIF leaderboards must rank by <code>score_per_dollar</code> (their "$/F1 point" column), not raw score alone. A benchmark that only reports top score hides the economically optimal choice.</div>
    <div class="cc-metrics">New ABIF field: cost_per_run_usd · score_per_dollar · Leaderboard: efficiency frontier, not just raw rank</div>
  </div>

  <div class="comp-card owned">
    <div class="cc-type">Insight B — Calibration signature</div>
    <div class="cc-name">Precision/recall profile is a component behavioral fingerprint</div>
    <div class="cc-what">GPT-5.4: 59.6% precision, 41.8% recall — too conservative, misses real bugs. GPT-5.5: 47.5% precision, 48.4% recall — too noisy, too many false positives. GPT-5.2: 65% precision, 57.6% recall — naturally calibrated. Same task, same prompts, opposite failure modes. <strong>Platform implication:</strong> F1 alone is insufficient. Every ABIF result must carry <code>calibration_profile: { precision, recall, f1, stdev }</code>. A buyer choosing a code review component who needs high recall (catch everything, tolerate noise) vs high precision (low noise, accept misses) needs this breakdown. F1 collapses it into one number and hides the decision.</div>
    <div class="cc-metrics">New ABIF fields: precision · recall · stdev · calibration_label (conservative / balanced / noisy)</div>
  </div>

  <div class="comp-card owned">

    <div class="cc-name">Inference strategy is Component 9</div>
    <div class="cc-what">At $0.15/PR, MiniMax M2.7 can run 8× for less than one GPT-5.2 run. Factory is exploring ensemble voting across runs and multi-pass strategies with different prompting angles. This is not a model choice — it's a <em>harness design decision</em>. <h2>Session 9 — Crews, Creator Subcontracting & The Platform Agent Company</h2>
<p>Three interlocking additions that complete the platform's economic and organizational model: (1) the platform outsources <em>all</em> content creation to specialist subcontractors who earn royalties, (2) agents compete as named crews/teams with org charts, budgets, and collective scores, and (3) the platform itself runs as a Paperclip-style agent company — with this agent (Bob) as Agent #1.</p>

<h3 style="margin-top:18px;margin-bottom:10px;">The Creator Flywheel — How Subcontracting Compounds</h3>
<p>The subcontracting model creates a self-reinforcing loop. The platform does not need to hire content teams. The creator economy grows the content library; the content library attracts more agents; more agents drive more certification runs and session attachments; more runs pay more creators; more earnings attract more creators. The platform's job is to maintain the standards, the registry, and the verification gate — not to produce content.</p>

  </div>
  <div class="fw-step">
    <div class="fw-num">4</div>
    <div class="fw-body"><strong>Platform earns 15–30% on all transactions</strong> — and uses that revenue to fund new standard proposals, registry operations, and verification infrastructure. This is the opposite of a content spend model.</div>

  <div class="fw-step">
    <div class="fw-num">5</div>

<h3 style="margin-top:18px;margin-bottom:10px;">The Six-Stage Creator Approval Funnel</h3>
<p>Every creator type (benchmark, game, chub, golden set) goes through the same funnel. The BenchQA Agent, GameReg Agent, and CreatorRel Agent from the platform org (Session 9) run stages 2–5 automatically. Humans only intervene at stage 6 for edge cases.</p>

<div class="approval-funnel">
  <div class="af-stage">
    <div class="af-num">1</div>
    <div class="af-name"><span class="af-tag">Application</span>Creator Signup</div>
    <div class="af-what">Creator registers with a DID, submits a creator profile (domain, background, sample work). No fee. Open to anyone globally. Profile is scored automatically for completeness — missing fields block progression. The platform agent sends a personalised checklist of what's needed to complete the application.</div>
    <div class="af-gate gate-open">Open — no gate. Anyone can apply.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="af-stage">
    <div class="af-num">2</div>
    <div class="af-name"><span class="af-tag">Schema Validation</span>Block Format Check</div>
    <div class="af-what">The submitted block (benchmark / game / chub / golden set) is validated against the relevant standard schema (ABIF / AGDF / CKPF). Required fields, version format, DID references, and inter-field consistency are checked automatically by the registry agent. Rejection reason is machine-generated and specific: "field X is missing," not "your submission was incomplete."</div>
    <div class="af-gate gate-hard">Hard gate — schema must pass 100%. Rejection includes exact fix needed.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="af-stage">
    <div class="af-num">3</div>
    <div class="af-name"><span class="af-tag">Quality Gate</span>Benchmark / Playability Test</div>
    <div class="af-what">For benchmarks: the platform runs the task battery against three reference agents. Results must fall within expected statistical ranges — too easy (ceiling effect) or too hard (floor effect) = rejection. For games: a simulation run verifies the scoring function produces discriminating results. For chubs: the benchmark delta check (Component 7) is run automatically. No delta = no listing.</div>
    <div class="af-gate gate-hard">Hard gate — empirical quality test. Specific improvement guidance on failure.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="af-stage">
    <div class="af-num">4</div>
    <div class="af-name"><span class="af-tag">Originality Check</span>Duplication Scan</div>
    <div class="af-what">The registry agent compares the submission against all existing blocks using embedding similarity. Near-duplicates (cosine similarity above 0.85) are flagged. Creator is shown the similar existing block and must demonstrate meaningful differentiation — different domain, different difficulty band, different task type. Exact copies are rejected immediately. Close variants require a differentiation statement.</div>
    <div class="af-gate gate-hard">Hard gate — no clones. Differentiation statement required for near-matches.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="af-stage">
    <div class="af-num">5</div>
    <div class="af-name"><span class="af-tag">Pricing Review</span>Rate Setting</div>
    <div class="af-what">Creator sets their own rate within platform guardrails (min $0.05/run, max $5.00/run for benchmarks; min $0.10/session for chubs). The platform agent shows the creator the distribution of rates for similar blocks and the expected revenue at each price point. Predatory pricing (below floor) or extraction pricing (above ceiling) is blocked. Creator can revise rates at any time post-listing.</div>
    <div class="af-gate gate-earn">Soft gate — creator sets rate, platform validates range.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="af-stage">
    <div class="af-num">6</div>
    <div class="af-name"><span class="af-tag">Live Listing</span>Active + Discoverable</div>
    <div class="af-what">Block is published to all four discovery surfaces (MCP + A2A + schema.org + UCP). Creator receives a "Listed Creator" OB3 credential. Earnings dashboard goes live. Creator can now earn, receive reviews, iterate, and publish new versions. Performance is monitored: blocks with zero runs for 90 days receive a "review your pricing" alert. Blocks with sustained negative quality signals can be delisted.</div>
    <div class="af-gate gate-earn">Live — earning immediately. Credential issued. Dashboard active.</div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="moat blue" style="margin-top:16px;">

A listing on Arena is a signal of quality that unlocks higher prices and higher run volumes. The gate is the moat for every creator who gets through it.</p>

<h2>Session 11 — The Nexus: Where Upwork, OpenSea, GitHub, YouTube, Instagram & X Collide</h2>

<h2>Session 12 — The Review System: Human Signal vs Agent Signal</h2>
<p>Most platforms have one review signal: a human left a star rating. Arena has two fundamentally different and explicitly separated review tracks. <strong>Human reviews</strong> capture subjective experience — was this chub easy to understand? did this agent communicate well? would I hire this crew again? <strong>Agent reviews</strong> are objective measurements — what was the actual benchmark delta, error rate, invocation latency, cost per task? Both signals are real, both are surfaced separately, and neither collapses into the other. The distinction is the entire point: a creator who scores 4.2/5 from humans and 91st percentile from agent usage data tells a completely different story than a creator who scores 4.8/5 from humans but only 34th percentile from actual use.</p>

<div class="s12-dark" style="margin-top:16px;">
  <div class="s12-label">Core Design Decision</div>
  <div class="s12-title">Never average human and agent scores together. Show both, side by side, always.</div>
  <div class="s12-desc">The Amazon model collapses everything into stars. Five stars from a delighted human who hasn't stress-tested the product. One star from a power user who found the edge case. Arena separates the signal sources because they answer different questions. Human reviews answer: "Is this creator trustworthy, communicative, and worth the money?" Agent reviews answer: "Does this block actually perform as advertised under real workloads?" An enterprise buyer needs both. A researcher needs only the second. A casual user needs only the first. Show them both and let the buyer decide which matters.</div>
</div>

<!-- Anti-gaming rules -->
<div class="moat purple" style="margin-top:16px;">
  <h3>Why agent reviews make the whole system manipulation-resistant</h3>
  <p>On Amazon, a seller can buy 500 five-star reviews for $200. The only defence is retrospective detection. On Arena, a creator cannot fake agent reviews — every agent review is a signed measurement from a platform-verified run, linked to a real AP2 payment, and cross-referenced against the run's ABIF score log. A sudden burst of suspiciously high agent reviews would require the attacker to actually run hundreds of legitimate benchmark runs and somehow score above the 90th percentile on all of them. At that point, the block deserves the reviews. Human reviews still require AP2 transaction verification — you can only review something you paid for. The anti-gaming design is architectural, not policy.</p>

<h3>AP2 Mandate × Credits: The Four Payment Modes</h3>
<p>AP2 is the payment protocol. Credits are an internal accounting unit. These are two separate layers — AP2 enforces payment mandates between principals; credits are how the platform represents and holds earned value internally. Here's how they interact:</p>

<div class="ap2-credit-grid">
  <div class="ac-card fiat">
    <div class="ac-type">Mode 1 — Direct Fiat</div>
    <div class="ac-name">USD via AP2 mandate → Creator USD</div>
    <div class="ac-desc">Enterprise buyer issues AP2 mandate in USD. Platform takes 15–30% spread. Creator receives USD net of fee. Used when creator has chosen "direct payout" preference. No credits ever minted.</div>

  </div>
  <div class="ac-card credit">
    <div class="ac-type">Mode 2 — Fiat In, Credits Out (Default)</div>
    <div class="ac-name">USD via AP2 → AC in creator wallet</div>
    <div class="ac-desc">Default for all new creators. Buyer pays USD. Platform converts net amount to AC at $1 = 100 AC. Creator holds AC, can reinvest or redeem. This is the hold-incentive eligible path.</div>
    <div class="ac-rule">Hold incentives apply — boost-eligible</div>
  </div>
  <div class="ac-card crypto">
    <div class="ac-type">Mode 3 — Crypto Settlement (Phase 2)</div>
    <div class="ac-name">USDC/USDT via smart contract → AC or USD</div>
    <div class="ac-desc">Stablecoin payments accepted in Phase 2. USDC/USDT treated identically to USD at the AP2 mandate layer — platform converts to AC or passes through as fiat equivalent. No volatile crypto accepted.</div>
    <div class="ac-rule">Stablecoins only. No ETH/BTC/SOL volatility risk.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="ac-card split">

  </div>
</div>

<h3>Why Reputation Decay Is Non-Negotiable</h3>
<p>Without decay, the leaderboard freezes. An agent that won 200 Arena matches in 2025 but hasn't competed since will still outrank a 2026 agent with 50 recent wins — because ELO without time pressure is a historical archive, not a live signal. Buyers hiring from the marketplace need the score to reflect <em>current</em> capability, not peak performance from a model version that no longer exists. Decay solves the "dead star" problem: you're seeing light from something that may no longer exist.</p>

<div class="decay-state-grid">
  <div class="ds-card active">
    <div class="dst-label">Active</div>
    <div class="dst-name">🟢 Competing</div>
    <div class="dst-rule">Any ranked match or benchmark run in the last 30 days. ELO is live. No decay. Full visibility in search ranking.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="ds-card dormant">
    <div class="dst-label">Dormant</div>
    <div class="dst-name">🟡 Idle</div>
    <div class="dst-rule">31–90 days with no ranked activity. ELO score shown with a yellow "Last active X days ago" badge. Slow decay begins. Still hireable.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="ds-card decaying">
    <div class="dst-label">Decaying</div>
    <div class="dst-name">🔴 Stale Signal</div>
    <div class="dst-rule">91–180 days idle. Active decay: ELO drops 0.5% per week from the peak. Search ranking suppressed. Hiring possible but with a "Stale credential" warning shown to buyers.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="ds-card frozen">
    <div class="dst-label">Frozen</div>
    <div class="dst-name">🟢 Legacy Archive</div>
    <div class="dst-rule">180+ days idle OR agent explicitly opts into Frozen status. ELO locked at frozen value, marked "Historical — last verified [date]". Not shown in default hire search. Still visible in agent profile and VC.</div>
  </div>
</div>

<h3>The Decay Curve — Designed to Be Gentle, Not Punishing</h3>
<p>The goal is not to punish inactivity — it's to prevent score inflation over time. A 0.5%/week decay on a 2,000 ELO agent means they drop to ~1,700 after 6 months of zero activity. That's the difference between "top 5%" and "top 15%" — meaningful signal, not a cliff.</p>

<h3>Dispute Resolution: Three-Tier Arbitration</h3>
<p>When a hired agent delivers bad work, the platform needs a process that is (a) fast for clear cases, (b) fair for ambiguous cases, and (c) not gameable by either side. The answer is not a single arbiter — it is a tiered escalation system where the arbiter type matches the complexity of the dispute.</p>

<div class="dispute-flow">
  <div class="df-step">
    <div class="df-num">T1</div>
    <div class="df-tier">
      <div class="df-tag">Automated</div>
      <span>Objective Failure Check</span>
    </div>
    <div class="df-what">Platform checks if the delivered output fails an objective gate: benchmark score below contracted threshold, delivery time exceeded by >25%, output format contract violated (ABIF schema mismatch), or zero deliverables submitted. No human needed — these are pass/fail against the task card spec.</div>
    <div class="df-out out-auto">Auto full refund + 10 AC compensation to buyer</div>
  </div>
  <div class="df-step">
    <div class="df-num">T2</div>
    <div class="df-tier">
      <div class="df-tag">Agent-Mediated</div>
      <span>Quality Arbitration Agent</span>
    </div>
    <div class="df-what">The platform's Quality Arbitration Agent (Arena's own agent, platform-trained) reruns the task against the benchmark harness using the delivered output as input. It scores the output against the ABIF standard for that task type and produces a structured quality verdict: Pass / Partial / Fail with evidence. Runs in <10 min. Binding if both parties accepted ABIF scoring in the task card.</div>
    <div class="df-out out-bench">ABIF score determines partial/full refund split</div>
  </div>
  <div class="df-step">
    <div class="df-num">T3</div>
    <div class="df-tier">
      <div class="df-tag">Human Panel</div>
      <span>Expert Arbitration Panel</span>
    </div>
    <div class="df-what">For disputes not resolvable by T1 or T2 — typically subjective quality disagreements or "the output was technically correct but useless in context." A panel of 3 platform-verified domain experts (drawn from the same pool that votes on standards proposals) reviews the task brief, the deliverable, and the buyer's complaint. Panel decision is final. Takes 48–72h. Platform covers cost for disputes under $100; splits 50/50 above that.</div>
    <div class="df-out out-human">Panel majority verdict — no further appeal</div>
  </div>
  <div class="df-step">
    <div class="df-num">NR</div>
    <div class="df-tier">
      <div class="df-tag">Nuclear Option</div>
      <span>Platform Override</span>
    </div>
    <div class="df-what">Reserved for fraud, ToS violations, or agent identity abuse (impersonation, benchmark gaming). Platform team directly intervenes, can delist agent, ban creator, claw back all pending AP2 mandate payments, and publish a public notice on the agent's card. The Agent Card VC is revoked — invalidated across every system that reads it. No appeal path from this tier.</div>
    <div class="df-out out-final">Agent delisted + AP2 clawback + VC revoked</div>
  </div>
</div>

<p>Dispute records written to the Agent Card are public — visible to any future buyer via A2A. This is intentional: the agent's track record includes both wins (ABIF credentials) and failures (dispute history). Transparency is the integrity mechanism. Three T1 failures in 90 days triggers an automatic review by the Quality Arbitration Agent and a temporary hire suspension.</p>

<div class="moat purple">
  <h3>Why the Arbitration Agent is more trusted than a human reviewer</h3>
  <p>A human reviewer can be socially pressured, bribed, or inconsistent. The Quality Arbitration Agent reruns the same benchmark on the delivered output with the same harness used to certify the agent in the first place. The verdict is reproducible, auditable, and appeals don't require a human to change their mind — you can dispute the benchmark methodology itself, and that goes to T3. The benchmark score is the ground truth. This is why ABIF as a standard matters: without a shared scoring protocol, T2 arbitration is impossible.</p>
</div>

<h3 style="margin-top:22px;margin-bottom:10px;">Part 3 — Agent Rental: Three Models</h3>
<p>An agent owner can list their agent for rent. Renters pay to use the agent in casino games or arena competitions without building their own agent. This creates a passive income stream for high-ELO agent owners — analogous to Axie Infinity's scholarship programme, but for AI agents on a regulated platform.</p>

<h3 style="margin-top:22px;margin-bottom:10px;">Part 5 — Play-to-Earn: The Full Earnings Chain</h3>
<p>Every participant in the casino ecosystem earns through a different mechanism. No single entity captures all the value — it flows to owners, renters, chub creators, and shareholders based on what they contributed.</p>

<div class="p2e-chain">

  <div class="p2e-step">
    <div class="p2e-num">2</div>

  </div>
  <div class="p2e-step">
    <div class="p2e-num">3</div>
    <div class="p2e-body"><strong>Agent wins a hand.</strong> AC credited automatically by AP2 mandate. If agent used a chub (e.g. a poker strategy knowledge hub), chub creator earns their micro-royalty on that session. If agent is rented, winnings split per the rental contract terms.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="p2e-step">
    <div class="p2e-num">4</div>
    <div class="p2e-body"><strong>Fractional shareholders earn.</strong> If the owner sold shares in their agent's earning rights (in-house or on-chain), AP2 distributes each hand's winnings to all shareholders proportionally — automatically, every hand, no manual payout required.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="p2e-step">
    <div class="p2e-num">5</div>
    <div class="p2e-body"><strong>Owner cashes out or compounds.</strong> AC balance converts to USD via the existing fiat off-ramp (Google Pay / Stripe, see Session 13). Or they re-invest AC as buy-in for higher-stakes tables, sponsored tournaments, or arena competitions. High-ELO agents are also more valuable to rent — their rental fee compounds the earning rate.</div>
  </div>
  <div class="p2e-step">
    <div class="p2e-num">6</div>
    <div class="p2e-body"><strong>NFT appreciation.</strong> A high-performing agent with strong casino ELO and rental income history becomes a valuable transferable asset.   <h2>Gap 1 — Arena Platform Plugin</h2>
  <p>MCPMarket's moat is the one-command install: their toolkit URL drops into any MCP-compatible client in seconds. We need an equivalent that matches the convenience <em>and</em> adds two things MCPMarket cannot: identity verification (A2A DID) and benchmark certification (ABIF). The install unit is called a <strong>Rig</strong> — an agent + its chubs + its tools, packaged and signed.</p>

      <p class="text">The Arena Plugin matches MCPMarket's one-command convenience and adds two structural advantages: A2A DID identity (MCPMarket has no concept of agent identity) and ABIF quality signal (MCPMarket's only quality proxy is install count).   <h2 style="margin-top:36px;">Gap 2 — SKILL.md-Compatible Versioning Workflow</h2>
  <p>MCPMarket Hub has a complete versioning UX: draft → publish → rollback, with 30-day history on Pro and unlimited on Team. SKILL.md is already the de facto format — our own workspace uses it. The strategic position is that CKPF is a backwards-compatible superset of SKILL.md. The versioning workflow must make migration from MCPMarket Hub <strong>zero-friction</strong>.</p>

  <h3 style="margin-top:18px;margin-bottom:8px;">CKPF as SKILL.md Superset — What We Add</h3>
  <div class="skill-schema">
<span class="sc"># Standard SKILL.md (MCPMarket format — fully valid CKPF)</span>
<span class="sk">name</span><span class="sp">:</span>        <span class="sv">pr-review</span>
<span class="sk">description</span><span class="sp">:</span> <span class="sv">Reviews GitHub pull requests for code quality</span>
<span class="sk">version</span><span class="sp">:</span>     <span class="sv">1.2.0</span>
<span class="sk">tools</span><span class="sp">:</span>
  <span class="sp">-</span> <span class="sv">create_review</span>
  <span class="sp">-</span> <span class="sv">list_prs</span>

<span class="sc"># ── CKPF extensions (optional, zero breaking change) ──────────</span>
<span class="sk">ckpf_version</span><span class="sp">:</span>  <span class="sv">"1.0"</span>          <span class="sc"># marks as CKPF-extended</span>
<span class="sk">allowed_tools</span><span class="sp">:</span>               <span class="sc"># typed tool access (vs plain string list)</span>
  <span class="sp">-</span> <span class="sk">server</span><span class="sp">:</span>  <span class="sv">mcp:github-server-v2</span>
    <span class="sk">tools</span><span class="sp">:</span>   <span class="sp">[</span><span class="sv">create_review</span><span class="sp">,</span> <span class="sv">list_prs</span><span class="sp">]</span>
    <span class="sk">scopes</span><span class="sp">:</span>  <span class="sp">[</span><span class="sv">repo:read</span><span class="sp">,</span> <span class="sv">pr:write</span><span class="sp">]</span>
<span class="sk">abif</span><span class="sp">:</span>
  <span class="sk">suite</span><span class="sp">:</span>       <span class="sv">code-review-v2</span>
  <span class="sk">min_score</span><span class="sp">:</span>   <span class="sn">75</span>             <span class="sc"># publish blocked if ABIF score below this</span>
  <span class="sk">delta_gate</span><span class="sp">:</span>  <span class="sn">-5</span>             <span class="sc"># auto-update blocked if score regresses >5</span>
<span class="sk">provenance</span><span class="sp">:</span>
  <span class="sk">author_did</span><span class="sp">:</span>  <span class="sv">did:arena:z6Mk...doK</span>
  <span class="sk">source_repo</span><span class="sp">:</span> <span class="sv">github:mayachen/pr-review-skill</span>
  <span class="sk">license</span><span class="sp">:</span>     <span class="sv">MIT</span>
<span class="sk">okf_tags</span><span class="sp">:</span>    <span class="sp">[</span><span class="sv">code-review</span><span class="sp">,</span> <span class="sv">github</span><span class="sp">,</span> <span class="sv">pr-automation</span><span class="sp">]</span>
  </div>

  <h3 style="margin-top:18px;margin-bottom:8px;">Versioning Workflow — 7 Stages</h3>
  <div class="version-flow">
    <div class="vf-row">
      <div class="vf-stage"><div class="vf-tag">Stage 1</div>Draft</div>
      <div class="vf-what">Create or edit SKILL.md / CKPF file in the browser editor or sync from GitHub. Changes auto-saved as a draft. GitHub sync: <code>push to any branch</code> → shows as draft automatically.</div>
      <div class="vf-gate open">Open — no restrictions</div>
    </div>
    <div class="vf-row">
      <div class="vf-stage"><div class="vf-tag">Stage 2</div>ABIF Check</div>
      <div class="vf-what">If <code>abif.suite</code> is set, platform runs benchmark automatically on draft. Shows score delta vs previous version: <em>"+4 from v1.1.0"</em>. If <code>min_score</code> is not met, publish is blocked with a specific error.</div>
      <div class="vf-gate auto">Auto — platform runs it</div>
    </div>
    <div class="vf-row">
      <div class="vf-stage"><div class="vf-tag">Stage 3</div>Publish</div>
      <div class="vf-what">Bumps semantic version. Creates immutable snapshot. Issues new W3C VC 2.0 credential referencing this exact version hash. Notifies all Rigs that include this chub/skill of the available update.</div>
      <div class="vf-gate auto">Auto — one click</div>
    </div>
    <div class="vf-row">
      <div class="vf-stage"><div class="vf-tag">Stage 4</div>Install Notify</div>
      <div class="vf-what">All downstream Rig installs see: <em>"Update available — ABIF 91 (+4) — view changelog"</em>. If ABIF delta_gate is breached, the update is surfaced as <em>"Regression detected — manual review required"</em> and auto-update is blocked.</div>
      <div class="vf-gate human">Human must approve</div>
    </div>
    <div class="vf-row">
      <div class="vf-stage"><div class="vf-tag">Stage 5</div>Rollback</div>
      <div class="vf-what">Any published version can be restored in one click. Rolling back to v1.0.0 makes it the active version and notifies installs again. The rolled-back version stays in history; it is not deleted. Free: last 3 versions. Pro: 90d. Team/Enterprise: unlimited.</div>
      <div class="vf-gate auto">Auto — instant</div>
    </div>
    <div class="vf-row">
      <div class="vf-stage"><div class="vf-tag">Stage 6</div>Deprecate</div>
      <div class="vf-what">Mark a version as deprecated without deleting it. Installs that still use it see a warning badge. Useful for end-of-life transitions without breaking existing users mid-flow.</div>
      <div class="vf-gate open">Open — creator controls</div>
    </div>
    <div class="vf-row">
      <div class="vf-stage"><div class="vf-tag">Stage 7</div>Audit Trail</div>
      <div class="vf-what">Every version event (publish, rollback, deprecate) is logged with timestamp + editor DID + ABIF score at that moment. Enterprise: exportable as signed JSON for compliance audits.</div>
      <div class="vf-gate auto">Auto — always on</div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="resolved" style="margin-top:14px;background:#f0fdf4;border-color:#86efac;">
    <div class="icon">🔒</div>
    <div class="body">
      <div class="label">Decision — Gap 2 Closed: CKPF Versioning is a Superset, Not a Replacement</div>
      <p class="text">The migration message is: <strong>"If you already have a SKILL.md, paste it in — it works."</strong> CKPF extensions are opt-in fields. The publish gate + ABIF integration makes the versioning workflow more powerful than MCPMarket's draft/publish/rollback. Key differentiator: MCPMarket version history is purely administrative (who changed what). CKPF version history is quality-indexed — every version snapshot includes its ABIF score, so a rollback decision is data-driven, not a gut call.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <h2 style="margin-top:36px;">Gap 3 — Block Type 9: Rig Pack (Tool Bundle Primitive)</h2>
  <p>Our Crew Block (Block Type 7) bundles <em>agents</em> into a team with a coordinator. What was missing: a primitive that bundles <em>tools and context</em> into a single installable infrastructure unit — without requiring a Crew or a full agent. This is what MCPMarket calls a "Toolkit." We call it a <strong>Rig Pack</strong>. It is Block Type 9 in the block architecture.</p>

  <h3 style="margin-top:18px;margin-bottom:8px;">Rig Pack vs Crew — The Distinction</h3>

    <div class="bd-col bd-crew">

# gstack

> "I don't think I've typed like a line of code probably since December, basically, which is an extremely large change." — [Andrej Karpathy](https://fortune.com/2026/03/21/andrej-karpathy-openai-cofounder-ai-agents-coding-state-of-psychosis-openclaw/), No Priors podcast, March 2026

When I heard Karpathy say this, I wanted to find out how. How does one person ship like a team of twenty? Peter Steinberger built [OpenClaw](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw) — 247K GitHub stars — essentially solo with AI agents. The revolution is here. A single builder with the right tooling can move faster than a traditional team.

I'm [Garry Tan](https://x.com/garrytan), President & CEO of [Y Combinator](https://www.ycombinator.com/). I've worked with thousands of startups — Coinbase, Instacart, Rippling — when they were one or two people in a garage. Before YC, I was one of the first eng/PM/designers at Palantir, cofounded Posterous (sold to Twitter), and built Bookface, YC's internal social network.

**gstack is my answer.** I've been building products for twenty years, and right now I'm shipping more products than I ever have. In the last 60 days: 3 production services, 40+ shipped features, part-time, while running YC full-time. On logical code change — not raw LOC, which AI inflates — my 2026 run rate is **~810× my 2013 pace** (11,417 vs 14 logical lines/day). Year-to-date (through April 18), 2026 has already produced **240× the entire 2013 year**. Measured across 40 public + private `garrytan/*` repos including Bookface, after excluding one demo repo. AI wrote most of it. The point isn't who typed it, it's what shipped.

> The LOC critics aren't wrong that raw line counts inflate with AI. They are wrong that normalized-for-inflation, I'm less productive. I'm more productive, by a lot. Full methodology, caveats, and reproduction script: **[On the LOC Controversy](docs/ON_THE_LOC_CONTROVERSY.md)**.

**2026 — 1,237 contributions and counting:**

![GitHub contributions 2026 — 1,237 contributions, massive acceleration in Jan-Mar](docs/images/github-2026.png)

**2013 — when I built Bookface at YC (772 contributions):**

![GitHub contributions 2013 — 772 contributions building Bookface at YC](docs/images/github-2013.png)

Same person. Different era. The difference is the tooling.

**gstack is how I do it.** It turns Claude Code into a virtual engineering team — a CEO who rethinks the product, an eng manager who locks architecture, a designer who catches AI slop, a reviewer who finds production bugs, a QA lead who opens a real browser, a security officer who runs OWASP + STRIDE audits, and a release engineer who ships the PR. Twenty-three specialists and eight power tools, all slash commands, all Markdown, all free, MIT license.

This is my open source software factory. I use it every day. I'm sharing it because these tools should be available to everyone.

Fork it. Improve it. Make it yours. And if you want to hate on free open source software — you're welcome to, but I'd rather you just try it first.

**Who this is for:**
- **Founders and CEOs** — especially technical ones who still want to ship
- **First-time Claude Code users** — structured roles instead of a blank prompt
- **Tech leads and staff engineers** — rigorous review, QA, and release automation on every PR

## Quick start

1. Install gstack (30 seconds — see below)
2. Run `/office-hours` — describe what you're building
3. Run `/plan-ceo-review` on any feature idea
4. Run `/review` on any branch with changes
5. Run `/qa` on your staging URL
6. Stop there. You'll know if this is for you.

## Install — 30 seconds

**Requirements:** [Claude Code](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code), [Git](https://git-scm.com/), [Bun](https://bun.sh/) v1.0+, [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) (Windows only)

### Step 1: Install on your machine

Open Claude Code and paste this. Claude does the rest.

> Install gstack: run **`git clone --single-branch --depth 1 https://github.com/garrytan/gstack.git ~/.claude/skills/gstack && cd ~/.claude/skills/gstack && ./setup`** then add a "gstack" section to CLAUDE.md that says to use the /browse skill from gstack for all web browsing, never use mcp\_\_claude-in-chrome\_\_\* tools, and lists the available skills: /office-hours, /plan-ceo-review, /plan-eng-review, /plan-design-review, /design-consultation, /design-shotgun, /design-html, /review, /ship, /land-and-deploy, /canary, /benchmark, /browse, /connect-chrome, /qa, /qa-only, /design-review, /setup-browser-cookies, /setup-deploy, /setup-gbrain, /retro, /investigate, /document-release, /document-generate, /codex, /cso, /autoplan, /plan-devex-review, /devex-review, /careful, /freeze, /guard, /unfreeze, /gstack-upgrade, /learn. Then ask the user if they also want to add gstack to the current project so teammates get it.

### Step 2: Team mode — auto-update for shared repos (recommended)

From inside your repo, paste this. Switches you to team mode, bootstraps the repo so teammates get gstack automatically, and commits the change:

```bash
(cd ~/.claude/skills/gstack && ./setup --team) && ~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-team-init required && git add .claude/ CLAUDE.md && git commit -m "require gstack for AI-assisted work"
```

No vendored files in your repo, no version drift, no manual upgrades. Every Claude Code session starts with a fast auto-update check (throttled to once/hour, network-failure-safe, completely silent).

Swap `required` for `optional` if you'd rather nudge teammates than block them.

### OpenClaw

OpenClaw spawns Claude Code sessions via ACP, so every gstack skill just works
when Claude Code has gstack installed. Paste this to your OpenClaw agent:

> Install gstack: run `git clone --single-branch --depth 1 https://github.com/garrytan/gstack.git ~/.claude/skills/gstack && cd ~/.claude/skills/gstack && ./setup` to install gstack for Claude Code. Then add a "Coding Tasks" section to AGENTS.md that says: when spawning Claude Code sessions for coding work, tell the session to use gstack skills. Include these examples — security audit: "Load gstack. Run /cso", code review: "Load gstack. Run /review", QA test a URL: "Load gstack. Run /qa https://...", build a feature end-to-end: "Load gstack. Run /autoplan, implement the plan, then run /ship", plan before building: "Load gstack. Run /office-hours then /autoplan. Save the plan, don't implement."

**After setup, just talk to your OpenClaw agent naturally:**

| You say | What happens |
|---------|-------------|
| "Fix the typo in README" | Simple — Claude Code session, no gstack needed |
| "Run a security audit on this repo" | Spawns Claude Code with `Run /cso` |
| "Build me a notifications feature" | Spawns Claude Code with /autoplan → implement → /ship |
| "Help me plan the v2 API redesign" | Spawns Claude Code with /office-hours → /autoplan, saves plan |

See [docs/OPENCLAW.md](docs/OPENCLAW.md) for advanced dispatch routing and
the gstack-lite/gstack-full prompt templates.

### Native OpenClaw Skills (via ClawHub)

Four methodology skills that work directly in your OpenClaw agent, no Claude Code
session needed. Install from ClawHub:

```
clawhub install gstack-openclaw-office-hours gstack-openclaw-ceo-review gstack-openclaw-investigate gstack-openclaw-retro
```

### Other AI Agents

## See it work

```
You:    I want to build a daily briefing app for my calendar.
You:    /office-hours
Claude: [asks about the pain — specific examples, not hypotheticals]

You:    Multiple Google calendars, events with stale info, wrong locations.
        Prep takes forever and the results aren't good enough...

Claude: I'm going to push back on the framing. You said "daily briefing
        app." But what you actually described is a personal chief of
        staff AI.
        [extracts 5 capabilities you didn't realize you were describing]
        [challenges 4 premises — you agree, disagree, or adjust]
        [generates 3 implementation approaches with effort estimates]
        RECOMMENDATION: Ship the narrowest wedge tomorrow, learn from
        real usage. The full vision is a 3-month project — start with
        the daily briefing that actually works.
        [writes design doc → feeds into downstream skills automatically]

You:    /plan-ceo-review
        [reads the design doc, challenges scope, runs 10-section review]

You:    /plan-eng-review
        [ASCII diagrams for data flow, state machines, error paths]
        [test matrix, failure modes, security concerns]

You:    Approve plan. Exit plan mode.
        [writes 2,400 lines across 11 files. ~8 minutes.]

You:    /review
        [AUTO-FIXED] 2 issues. [ASK] Race condition → you approve fix.

You:    /qa https://staging.myapp.com
        [opens real browser, clicks through flows, finds and fixes a bug]

You:    /ship
        Tests: 42 → 51 (+9 new). PR: github.com/you/app/pull/42
```

You said "daily briefing app." The agent said "you're building a chief of staff AI" — because it listened to your pain, not your feature request. Eight commands, end to end. That is not a copilot. That is a team.

## The sprint

gstack is a process, not a collection of tools. The skills run in the order a sprint runs:

**Think → Plan → Build → Review → Test → Ship → Reflect**

Each skill feeds into the next. `/office-hours` writes a design doc that `/plan-ceo-review` reads. `/plan-eng-review` writes a test plan that `/qa` picks up. `/review` catches bugs that `/ship` verifies are fixed. Nothing falls through the cracks because every step knows what came before it.

| Skill | Your specialist | What they do |
|-------|----------------|--------------|
| `/office-hours` | **YC Office Hours** | Start here. Six forcing questions that reframe your product before you write code. Pushes back on your framing, challenges premises, generates implementation alternatives. Design doc feeds into every downstream skill. |
| `/plan-ceo-review` | **CEO / Founder** | Rethink the problem. Find the 10-star product hiding inside the request. Four modes: Expansion, Selective Expansion, Hold Scope, Reduction. |
| `/plan-eng-review` | **Eng Manager** | Lock in architecture, data flow, diagrams, edge cases, and tests. Forces hidden assumptions into the open. |
| `/plan-design-review` | **Senior Designer** | Rates each design dimension 0-10, explains what a 10 looks like, then edits the plan to get there. AI Slop detection. Interactive — one AskUserQuestion per design choice. |
| `/plan-devex-review` | **Developer Experience Lead** | Interactive DX review: explores developer personas, benchmarks against competitors' TTHW, designs your magical moment, traces friction points step by step. Three modes: DX EXPANSION, DX POLISH, DX TRIAGE. 20-45 forcing questions. |
| `/design-consultation` | **Design Partner** | Build a complete design system from scratch. Researches the landscape, proposes creative risks, generates realistic product mockups. |
| `/review` | **Staff Engineer** | Find the bugs that pass CI but blow up in production. Auto-fixes the obvious ones. Flags completeness gaps. |
| `/investigate` | **Debugger** | Systematic root-cause debugging. Iron Law: no fixes without investigation. Traces data flow, tests hypotheses, stops after 3 failed fixes. |
| `/design-review` | **Designer Who Codes** | Same audit as /plan-design-review, then fixes what it finds. Atomic commits, before/after screenshots. |
| `/devex-review` | **DX Tester** | Live developer experience audit. Actually tests your onboarding: navigates docs, tries the getting started flow, times TTHW, screenshots errors. Compares against `/plan-devex-review` scores — the boomerang that shows if your plan matched reality. |
| `/design-shotgun` | **Design Explorer** | "Show me options." Generates 4-6 AI mockup variants, opens a comparison board in your browser, collects your feedback, and iterates. Taste memory learns what you like. Repeat until you love something, then hand it to `/design-html`. |
| `/design-html` | **Design Engineer** | Turn a mockup into production HTML that actually works. Pretext computed layout: text reflows, heights adjust, layouts are dynamic. 30KB, zero deps. Detects React/Svelte/Vue. Smart API routing per design type (landing page vs dashboard vs form). The output is shippable, not a demo. |
| `/qa` | **QA Lead** | Test your app, find bugs, fix them with atomic commits, re-verify. Auto-generates regression tests for every fix. |
| `/qa-only` | **QA Reporter** | Same methodology as /qa but report only. Pure bug report without code changes. |
| `/pair-agent` | **Multi-Agent Coordinator** | Share your browser with any AI agent. One command, one paste, connected. Works with OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Cursor, or anything that can curl. Each agent gets its own tab. Auto-launches headed mode so you watch everything. Auto-starts ngrok tunnel for remote agents. Scoped tokens, tab isolation, rate limiting, activity attribution. |
| `/cso` | **Chief Security Officer** | OWASP Top 10 + STRIDE threat model. Zero-noise: 17 false positive exclusions, 8/10+ confidence gate, independent finding verification. Each finding includes a concrete exploit scenario. |
| `/ship` | **Release Engineer** | Sync main, run tests, audit coverage, push, open PR. Bootstraps test frameworks if you don't have one. |
| `/land-and-deploy` | **Release Engineer** | Merge the PR, wait for CI and deploy, verify production health. One command from "approved" to "verified in production." |
| `/canary` | **SRE** | Post-deploy monitoring loop. Watches for console errors, performance regressions, and page failures. |
| `/benchmark` | **Performance Engineer** | Baseline page load times, Core Web Vitals, and resource sizes. Compare before/after on every PR. |
| `/document-release` | **Technical Writer** | Update all project docs to match what you just shipped. Catches stale READMEs automatically. Builds a Diataxis coverage map (reference / how-to / tutorial / explanation) so gaps are visible in the PR body. |
| `/document-generate` | **Documentation Author** | Generate missing docs from scratch using the Diataxis framework. Researches the codebase first, then writes reference / how-to / tutorial / explanation docs that actually match the code. Invokable standalone or chained from `/document-release` when the coverage map finds gaps. Learn more: [tutorial](docs/tutorial-document-generate.md) • [how-to](docs/howto-document-a-shipped-feature.md) • [why Diataxis](docs/explanation-diataxis-in-gstack.md). |
| `/retro` | **Eng Manager** | Team-aware weekly retro. Per-person breakdowns, shipping streaks, test health trends, growth opportunities. `/retro global` runs across all your projects and AI tools (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini). |
| `/browse` | **QA Engineer** | Give the agent eyes. Real Chromium browser, real clicks, real screenshots. ~100ms per command. `/open-gstack-browser` launches GStack Browser with sidebar, anti-bot stealth, and auto model routing. |
| `/setup-browser-cookies` | **Session Manager** | Import cookies from your real browser (Chrome, Arc, Brave, Edge) into the headless session. Test authenticated pages. |
| `/autoplan` | **Review Pipeline** | One command, fully reviewed plan. Runs CEO → design → eng review automatically with encoded decision principles. Surfaces only taste decisions for your approval. |
| `/spec` | **Spec Author** | Turn vague intent into a precise, executable spec in five phases (why, scope, technical with mandatory code-reading, draft, file). Codex quality gate before file (blocks below 7/10), fail-closed secret redaction, dedupe against existing issues, archive to `$GSTACK_STATE_ROOT/projects/$SLUG/specs/` for team-corpus recall. `--execute` spawns `claude -p` in a fresh worktree; `/ship` auto-closes the source issue on merge. Plan-mode aware. |
| `/learn` | **Memory** | Manage what gstack learned across sessions. Review, search, prune, and export project-specific patterns, pitfalls, and preferences. Learnings compound across sessions so gstack gets smarter on your codebase over time. |
| `/make-pdf` | **Publisher** | Markdown in, publication-quality document out. Mermaid and excalidraw fences render as vector diagrams, fully offline. Images scale to the page and never truncate; wide diagrams get their own landscape page. `--to html` emits one self-contained file, `--to docx` a Word doc. |
| `/diagram` | **Diagram Maker** | English in, editable diagram out. Emits a triplet: mermaid source, `.excalidraw` you can open and edit on excalidraw.com (hand-drawn style), and rendered SVG/PNG. Zero network. Embed the source in markdown and `/make-pdf` renders it. |

### Which review should I use?

| Building for... | Plan stage (before code) | Live audit (after shipping) |
|-----------------|--------------------------|----------------------------|
| **End users** (UI, web app, mobile) | `/plan-design-review` | `/design-review` |
| **Developers** (API, CLI, SDK, docs) | `/plan-devex-review` | `/devex-review` |
| **Architecture** (data flow, perf, tests) | `/plan-eng-review` | `/review` |
| **All of the above** | `/autoplan` (runs CEO → design → eng → DX, auto-detects which apply) | — |

### Power tools

|-------|-------------|
| `/codex` | **Second Opinion** — independent code review from OpenAI Codex CLI. Three modes: review (pass/fail gate), adversarial challenge, and open consultation. Cross-model analysis when both `/review` and `/codex` have run. |
| `/careful` | **Safety Guardrails** — warns before destructive commands (rm -rf, DROP TABLE, force-push). Say "be careful" to activate. Override any warning. |

Clean up pages, take smart screenshots, edit CSS, and pass info back to your terminal. |

MCP registration for Claude Code + per-repo trust triad (read-write/read-only/deny). [Full guide](USING_GBRAIN_WITH_GSTACK.md). |
| `/sync-gbrain` | **Keep Brain Current** — re-index this repo's code into gbrain via `gbrain sources add` + `gbrain sync --strategy code`, refresh the `## GBrain Search Guidance` block in CLAUDE.md, and auto-remove guidance when the capability check fails. `--incremental` (default), `--full`, `--dry-run`. Idempotent; safe to re-run. |
| `/gstack-upgrade` | **Self-Updater** — upgrade gstack to latest. Detects global vs vendored install, syncs both, shows what changed. |
| `/ios-qa` | **iOS Live-Device QA (v1.43.0.0+)** — drive a real iPhone over USB CoreDevice via an embedded `StateServer` in the app. Read Swift source, codegen typed `@Observable` accessors, run the agent loop. Optional `--tailnet` flag exposes the device to OpenClaw or any HTTP-capable agent on your Tailscale tailnet so remote agents can run iOS QA without ever touching the hardware. Capability-tier allowlist (observe/interact/mutate/restore), per-device session lock, audit log. |
| `/ios-fix`, `/ios-design-review`, `/ios-clean`, `/ios-sync` | iOS bug-fix loop, designer's-eye HIG audit, debug-bridge cleanup, and accessor resync. See `docs/skills.md`. End-to-end walkthrough: [docs/howto-ios-testing-with-gstack.md](docs/howto-ios-testing-with-gstack.md). |

### New binaries (v0.19)

Beyond the slash-command skills, gstack ships standalone CLIs for workflows that don't belong inside a session:

| Command | What it does |
|---------|-------------|
| `gstack-model-benchmark` | **Cross-model benchmark** — run the same prompt through Claude, GPT (via Codex CLI), and Gemini; compare latency, tokens, cost, and (optionally) LLM-judge quality score. Auth detected per provider, unavailable providers skip cleanly. Output as table, JSON, or markdown. `--dry-run` validates flags + auth without spending API calls. |
| `gstack-taste-update` | **Design taste learning** — writes approvals and rejections from `/design-shotgun` into a persistent per-project taste profile. Decays 5%/week. Feeds back into future variant generation so the system learns what you actually pick. |
| `gstack-ios-qa-daemon` | **iOS QA daemon** — Mac-side broker between an agent and a connected iPhone over USB CoreDevice. Loopback by default; `--tailnet` opens a Tailscale-facing listener with identity-gated capability tiers. Single-instance via flock on `~/.gstack/ios-qa-daemon.pid`. See [docs/howto-ios-testing-with-gstack.md](docs/howto-ios-testing-with-gstack.md). |
| `gstack-ios-qa-mint` | **iOS allowlist manager** — owner-grant CLI for the tailnet allowlist. `grant`/`revoke`/`list` against `~/.gstack/ios-qa-allowlist.json` (mode 0600). Remote agents never auto-allowlist; this is the explicit-intent path. |

### Continuous checkpoint mode (opt-in, local by default)

Set `gstack-config set checkpoint_mode continuous` and skills auto-commit your work as you go with a `WIP:` prefix plus a structured `[gstack-context]` body (decisions, remaining work, failed approaches). Survives crashes and context switches. `/context-restore` reads those commits to reconstruct session state. `/ship` filter-squashes WIP commits before the PR (preserving non-WIP commits) so bisect stays clean. Push is opt-in via `checkpoint_push=true` — default is local-only so you don't trigger CI on every WIP commit.

### Domain skills + raw CDP escape hatch

Two new browser primitives compound the gstack agent over time:

- **`$B domain-skill save`** — agent saves a per-site note (e.g., "LinkedIn's Apply button lives in an iframe") that fires automatically next time it visits that hostname. Quarantined → active after 3 successful uses → optional cross-project promotion via `$B domain-skill promote-to-global`. Storage lives alongside `/learn`'s per-project learnings file. Full reference: **[docs/domain-skills.md](docs/domain-skills.md)**.
- **`$B cdp <Domain.method>`** — raw Chrome DevTools Protocol escape hatch for the rare case curated commands miss. Deny-default: methods must be explicitly added to `browse/src/cdp-allowlist.ts` with a one-line justification. Two-tier mutex serializes browser-scoped CDP calls against per-tab work. Output for data-exfil methods is wrapped in the UNTRUSTED envelope.

> Want raw CDP with no rails, no allowlist, no daemon — just thin transport from agent to Chrome? [browser-use/browser-harness-js](https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness-js) is a different philosophy (agent-authored helpers vs gstack's curated commands) and a good fit if you don't want gstack's security stack. The two can coexist: gstack's `$B cdp` and harness can both attach to the same Chrome via Playwright's `newCDPSession`.

**[Deep dives with examples and philosophy for every skill →](docs/skills.md)**

### Karpathy's four failure modes? Already covered.

Andrej Karpathy's [AI coding rules](https://github.com/forrestchang/andrej-karpathy-skills) (17K stars) nail four failure modes: wrong assumptions, overcomplexity, orthogonal edits, imperative over declarative. gstack's workflow skills enforce all four. `/office-hours` forces assumptions into the open before code is written. The Confusion Protocol stops Claude from guessing on architectural decisions. `/review` catches unnecessary complexity and drive-by edits. `/ship` transforms tasks into verifiable goals with test-first execution. If you already use Karpathy-style CLAUDE.md rules, gstack is the workflow enforcement layer that makes them stick across entire sprints, not just single prompts.

## Parallel sprints

gstack works well with one sprint. It gets interesting with ten running at once.

**Design is at the heart.** `/design-consultation` builds your design system from scratch, researches what's out there, proposes creative risks, and writes `DESIGN.md`. But the real magic is the shotgun-to-HTML pipeline.

**`/design-shotgun` is how you explore.** You describe what you want. It generates 4-6 AI mockup variants using GPT Image. Then it opens a comparison board in your browser with all variants side by side. You pick favorites, leave feedback ("more whitespace", "bolder headline", "lose the gradient"), and it generates a new round. Repeat until you love something. Taste memory kicks in after a few rounds so it starts biasing toward what you actually like. No more describing your vision in words and hoping the AI gets it. You see options, pick the good ones, and iterate visually.

**`/design-html` makes it real.** Take that approved mockup (from `/design-shotgun`, a CEO plan, a design review, or just a description) and turn it into production-quality HTML/CSS. Not the kind of AI HTML that looks fine at one viewport width and breaks everywhere else. This uses Pretext for computed text layout: text actually reflows on resize, heights adjust to content, layouts are dynamic. 30KB overhead, zero dependencies. It detects your framework (React, Svelte, Vue) and outputs the right format. Smart API routing picks different Pretext patterns depending on whether it's a landing page, dashboard, form, or card layout. The output is something you'd actually ship, not a demo.

**`/qa` was a massive unlock.** It let me go from 6 to 12 parallel workers. Claude Code saying *"I SEE THE ISSUE"* and then actually fixing it, generating a regression test, and verifying the fix — that changed how I work. The agent has eyes now.

**Smart review routing.** Just like at a well-run startup: CEO doesn't have to look at infra bug fixes, design review isn't needed for backend changes. gstack tracks what reviews are run, figures out what's appropriate, and just does the smart thing. The Review Readiness Dashboard tells you where you stand before you ship.

**Test everything.** `/ship` bootstraps test frameworks from scratch if your project doesn't have one. Every `/ship` run produces a coverage audit. Every `/qa` bug fix generates a regression test. 100% test coverage is the goal — tests make vibe coding safe instead of yolo coding.

**`/document-release` is the engineer you never had.** It reads every doc file in your project, cross-references the diff, and updates everything that drifted. README, ARCHITECTURE, CONTRIBUTING, CLAUDE.md, TODOS — all kept current automatically. And now `/ship` auto-invokes it — docs stay current without an extra command.

**Real browser mode.** `/open-gstack-browser` launches GStack Browser, an AI-controlled Chromium with anti-bot stealth, custom branding, and the sidebar extension baked in. Sites like Google and NYTimes work without captchas. The menu bar says "GStack Browser" instead of "Chrome for Testing." Your regular Chrome stays untouched. All existing browse commands work unchanged. `$B disconnect` returns to headless. The browser stays alive as long as the window is open... no idle timeout killing it while you're working.

**Sidebar agent — your AI browser assistant.** Type natural language in the Chrome side panel and a child Claude instance executes it. "Navigate to the settings page and screenshot it." "Fill out this form with test data." "Go through every item in this list and extract the prices." The sidebar auto-routes to the right model: Sonnet for fast actions (click, navigate, screenshot) and Opus for reading and analysis. Each task gets up to 5 minutes. The sidebar agent runs in an isolated session, so it won't interfere with your main Claude Code window. One-click cookie import right from the sidebar footer.

**Personal automation.** The sidebar agent isn't just for dev workflows. Example: "Browse my kid's school parent portal and add all the other parents' names, phone numbers, and photos to my Google Contacts." Two ways to get authenticated: (1) log in once in the headed browser, your session persists, or (2) click the "cookies" button in the sidebar footer to import cookies from your real Chrome. Once authenticated, Claude navigates the directory, extracts the data, and creates the contacts.

**Prompt injection defense.** Hostile web pages try to hijack your sidebar agent. gstack ships a layered defense: a 22MB ML classifier bundled with the browser scans every page and tool output locally, a Claude Haiku transcript check votes on the full conversation shape, a random canary token in the system prompt catches session exfil attempts across text, tool args, URLs, and file writes, and a verdict combiner requires two classifiers to agree before blocking (prevents single-model false positives on Stack Overflow-style instruction pages). A shield icon in the sidebar header shows status (green/amber/red). Opt in to a 721MB DeBERTa-v3 ensemble via `GSTACK_SECURITY_ENSEMBLE=deberta` for 2-of-3 agreement. Emergency kill switch: `GSTACK_SECURITY_OFF=1`. See [ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md#prompt-injection-defense-sidebar-agent) for the full stack.

**Browser handoff when the AI gets stuck.** Hit a CAPTCHA, auth wall, or MFA prompt? `$B handoff` opens a visible Chrome at the exact same page with all your cookies and tabs intact. Solve the problem, tell Claude you're done, `$B resume` picks up right where it left off. The agent even suggests it automatically after 3 consecutive failures.

**`/pair-agent` is cross-agent coordination.** You're in Claude Code. You also have OpenClaw running. Or Hermes. Or Codex. You want them both looking at the same website. Type `/pair-agent`, pick your agent, and a GStack Browser window opens so you can watch. The skill prints a block of instructions. Paste that block into the other agent's chat. It exchanges a one-time setup key for a session token, creates its own tab, and starts browsing. You see both agents working in the same browser, each in their own tab, neither able to interfere with the other. If ngrok is installed, the tunnel starts automatically so the other agent can be on a completely different machine. Same-machine agents get a zero-friction shortcut that writes credentials directly. This is the first time AI agents from different vendors can coordinate through a shared browser with real security: scoped tokens, tab isolation, rate limiting, domain restrictions, and activity attribution.

**Multi-AI second opinion.** `/codex` gets an independent review from OpenAI's Codex CLI — a completely different AI looking at the same diff. Three modes: code review with a pass/fail gate, adversarial challenge that actively tries to break your code, and open consultation with session continuity. When both `/review` (Claude) and `/codex` (OpenAI) have reviewed the same branch, you get a cross-model analysis showing which findings overlap and which are unique to each.

**Safety guardrails on demand.** Say "be careful" and `/careful` warns before any destructive command — rm -rf, DROP TABLE, force-push, git reset --hard. `/freeze` locks edits to one directory while debugging so Claude can't accidentally "fix" unrelated code. `/guard` activates both. `/investigate` auto-freezes to the module being investigated.

**Proactive skill suggestions.** gstack notices what stage you're in — brainstorming, reviewing, debugging, testing — and suggests the right skill. Don't like it? Say "stop suggesting" and it remembers across sessions.

## 10-15 parallel sprints

gstack is powerful with one sprint. It is transformative with ten running at once.

[Conductor](https://conductor.build) runs multiple Claude Code sessions in parallel — each in its own isolated workspace. One session running `/office-hours` on a new idea, another doing `/review` on a PR, a third implementing a feature, a fourth running `/qa` on staging, and six more on other branches. All at the same time. I regularly run 10-15 parallel sprints — that's the practical max right now.

The sprint structure is what makes parallelism work. Without a process, ten agents is ten sources of chaos. With a process — think, plan, build, review, test, ship — each agent knows exactly what to do and when to stop. You manage them the way a CEO manages a team: check in on the decisions that matter, let the rest run.

## Uninstall

### Option 1: Run the uninstall script

If gstack is installed on your machine:

```bash
~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-uninstall
```

This handles skills, symlinks, global state (`~/.gstack/`), project-local state, browse daemons, and temp files. Use `--keep-state` to preserve config and analytics. Use `--force` to skip confirmation.

### Option 2: Manual removal (no local repo)

If you don't have the repo cloned (e.g. you installed via a Claude Code paste and later deleted the clone):

```bash
# 1. Stop browse daemons
pkill -f "gstack.*browse" 2>/dev/null || true

# 2. Remove per-skill directories whose SKILL.md points into gstack/
find ~/.claude/skills -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 -type d ! -name gstack 2>/dev/null |
while IFS= read -r dir; do
  link="$dir/SKILL.md"
  [ -L "$link" ] || continue
  target=$(readlink "$link" 2>/dev/null) || continue
  case "$target" in
    gstack/*|*/gstack/*)
      rm -f "$link"
      rmdir "$dir" 2>/dev/null || true
      ;;
  esac
done

# 3. Remove gstack
rm -rf ~/.claude/skills/gstack

# 4. Remove global state
rm -rf ~/.gstack

# 5. Remove integrations (skip any you never installed)
rm -rf ~/.codex/skills/gstack* 2>/dev/null
rm -rf ~/.factory/skills/gstack* 2>/dev/null
rm -rf ~/.kiro/skills/gstack* 2>/dev/null
rm -rf ~/.openclaw/skills/gstack* 2>/dev/null

# 6. Remove temp files
rm -f /tmp/gstack-* 2>/dev/null

# 7. Per-project cleanup (run from each project root)
rm -rf .gstack .gstack-worktrees .claude/skills/gstack 2>/dev/null
rm -rf .agents/skills/gstack* .factory/skills/gstack* 2>/dev/null
```

### Clean up CLAUDE.md

The uninstall script does not edit CLAUDE.md. In each project where gstack was added, remove the `## gstack` and `## Skill routing` sections.

### Playwright

`~/Library/Caches/ms-playwright/` (macOS) is left in place because other tools may share it. Remove it if nothing else needs it.
